")) } fn unfit(headers: &HeaderMap) -> Option<&str> { // A value comes back as it went in when it is text on one line. let fits = |value: &[u8]| str::from_utf8(value).is_ok_and(|text| !text.contains('
')); headers .iter() .find(|(_, value)| !fits(value)) .map(|(name, _)| name) } } #[derive(Inbox, sqlx::FromRow)] #[inbox(table = "export_jobs")] struct ExportJob { #[field(id, generated)] id: i64, #[field(processed_at)] processed_at: Option<DateTime<Utc>>, #[field(locked_until)] locked_until: Option<DateTime<Utc>>, #[field(headers)] meta: Lines, #[field(payload)] payload: Vec<u8>, } impl Publish<Sqlite> for ExportJob { async fn publish( conn: &mut SqliteConnection, message: &OutgoingMessage<'_>, ) -> Result<(), sqlx::Error> { // The column keeps the message's headers as the delivery reads them back. let headers = Lines::from_headers(message.headers()); sqlx::query("INSERT INTO export_jobs (meta, payload) VALUES (?, ?)") .bind(headers) .bind(message.payload()) .execute(conn) .await?; Ok(()) } } examples/manual/sqlx_headers_column.rs use ruststream::HeaderMap; use ruststream_sqlx::HeaderColumn; /// Headers kept one per line, `name: value`, in a `TEXT` column. #[derive(sqlx::Type)] #[sqlx(transparent)] struct Lines(String); impl HeaderColumn for Lines { fn take_headers(&mut self) -> HeaderMap { let headers = self .0 .lines() .filter_map(|line| line.split_once(": ")) .map(|(name, value)| (name.to_owned(), value.to_owned())) .collect(); self.0.clear(); headers } fn from_headers(headers: &HeaderMap) -> Self { let lines: Vec<String> = headers .iter() .map(|(name, value)| format!("{name}: {}", String::from_utf8_lossy(value))) .collect(); Self(lines.join("
")) } fn unfit(headers: &HeaderMap) -> Option<&str> { // A value comes back as it went in when it is text on one line. let fits = |value: &[u8]| str::from_utf8(value).is_ok_and(|text| !text.contains('
')); headers .iter() .find(|(_, value)| !fits(value)) .map(|(name, _)| name) } } #[derive(sqlx::FromRow)] struct ExportJob { id: i64, meta: Lines, payload: Vec<u8>, } impl InboxTable for ExportJob { type Id = i64; type Table = InboxSpec<( ProcessedAt<DateTime<Utc>>, Lease<DateTime<Utc>>, HeadersColumn, Payload, )>; const TABLE: Self::Table = InboxSpec::new("export_jobs", Column::new("id").generated()) .processed_at(Column::new("processed_at")) .lease(Column::new("locked_until")) .headers(Column::new("meta")) .payload(Column::new("payload")); fn id(&self) -> &i64 { &self.id } } impl HeaderRow for ExportJob { type Column = Lines; fn headers_mut(&mut self) -> &mut Lines { &mut self.meta } } impl Publish<Sqlite> for ExportJob { async fn publish( conn: &mut SqliteConnection, message: &OutgoingMessage<'_>, ) -> Result<(), sqlx::Error> { // The column keeps the message's headers as the delivery reads them back. let headers = Lines::from_headers(message.headers()); sqlx::query("INSERT INTO export_jobs (meta, payload) VALUES (?, ?)") .bind(headers) .bind(message.payload()) .execute(conn) .await?; Ok(()) } }

Each field of a headers struct without a role is a header: strings and bytes as they are, numbers in decimal, times in RFC 3339, None left out. The header's name is the field's column name, as sqlx's rename and rename_all set it. Its value comes from HeaderField: Field type Header value String, Vec<u8> its bytes integers, bool its decimal text, true or false chrono::DateTime<Utc> (feature chrono), time::OffsetDateTime (feature time) its RFC 3339 text Option<T> the value of T; None leaves the header out A service implements HeaderField for a type of its own. A field of a type without it does not compile, and the error offers the impl or a role. The fields that play a role are not headers: the handler reads them on the message. The header map is built on the first read of the delivery's headers, by middleware or an extractor such as Headers<T>, and a delivery whose headers nobody reads never builds it. A message published into the table through a repository carries only the headers the headers struct names, and a publish with another header fails with SqlxBrokerError::Header, so no header is lost on the way into the table. By hand, HeaderFields builds the map with put_header, which writes each value through its HeaderField.

A shipment's headers are a carrier of the service's own type, an order number, a flag, a time and an optional trace; the handler writes them to an audit table as the header map holds them. Macros Manual examples/sqlx_headers_field.rs use ruststream_sqlx::HeaderField; #[derive(Debug, Clone, InboxHeaders, sqlx::FromRow)] #[inbox(table = "shipment_jobs")] struct ShipmentHeaders { #[field(id, generated)] job_id: i64, #[field(locked_until)] locked_until: Option<DateTime<Utc>>, // Each field without a role is a header named after its column. carrier: Carrier, order_id: i64, express: bool, placed_at: DateTime<Utc>, trace: Option<String>, } /// A carrier, kept by its code in the table and named in capitals in the header. #[derive(Debug, Clone, sqlx::Type)] #[sqlx(transparent)] struct Carrier(String); impl HeaderField for Carrier { fn header(&self) -> Option<Vec<u8>> { Some(self.0.to_uppercase().into_bytes()) } } examples/manual/sqlx_headers_field.rs use ruststream::HeaderMap; use ruststream_sqlx::{HeaderField, HeaderFields, put_header}; #[derive(Debug, Clone, sqlx::FromRow, JsonSchema)] #[schemars(crate = "ruststream::schemars")] struct Shipment { job_id: i64, carrier: Carrier, order_id: i64, express: bool, #[schemars(with = "String")] placed_at: DateTime<Utc>, trace: Option<String>, } impl HeaderFields for Shipment { const NAMES: &'static [&'static str] = &["carrier", "order_id", "express", "placed_at", "trace"]; fn header_map(&self) -> HeaderMap { let mut headers = HeaderMap::with_capacity(Self::NAMES.len()); put_header(&mut headers, "carrier", &self.carrier); put_header(&mut headers, "order_id", &self.order_id); put_header(&mut headers, "express", &self.express); put_header(&mut headers, "placed_at", &self.placed_at); put_header(&mut headers, "trace", &self.trace); headers } } /// A carrier, kept by its code in the table and named in capitals in the header. #[derive(Debug, Clone, sqlx::Type, JsonSchema)] #[schemars(crate = "ruststream::schemars")] #[sqlx(transparent)] struct Carrier(String); impl HeaderField for Carrier { fn header(&self) -> Option<Vec<u8>> { Some(self.0.to_uppercase().into_bytes()) } }

In the headers layout a headers struct describes the queue table and its header fields, and the message struct that flattens it is what a handler takes. Two structs describe one queue. The headers struct derives InboxHeaders and describes the table: #[inbox(table, schema, advisory_lock, clock, isolation, mode)] and the fields that play a role, so it also selects the form. Its other fields are the delivery's header values. The message struct derives Inbox and holds the headers struct in a field marked #[field(headers)] and #[sqlx(flatten)], beside data of its own. It takes #[inbox(custom(..))] alone, and a role or a table attribute on it does not compile, with an error that names the headers struct as the place for it. The headers layout is row mode: a handler takes the message struct itself, or a slice of them in a batch. Several message structs may flatten one headers struct, each read by its own subscriptions. The claim selects the ids of the rows it takes, and the default fetch reads their rows from the queue table, the headers struct's columns and the message's own fields. A subscription prepares that fetch when it opens, so a message field whose column the table lacks stops startup with SqlxBrokerError::Schema. A message whose data lives in other tables reads it with a fetch of its own. The headers struct gets the generated insert, and the message struct gets none. By hand, one description on the message holds the whole table: .data(..) names the header columns, .fetching(..) the message's own, and .header_fields() builds the header map through HeaderFields and put_header.

A packing job: OrderHeaders describes order_jobs and its headers tenant, trace and order_id, and OrderJob adds the job's note. Macros Manual examples/sqlx_headers_layout.rs /// The queue table: the columns that run the queue, and the headers `tenant`, `trace` and /// `order_id`. #[derive(Debug, Clone, InboxHeaders, sqlx::FromRow)] #[inbox(table = "order_jobs")] struct OrderHeaders { #[field(id, generated)] job_id: i64, #[field(attempt, generated)] attempt: i16, #[field(locked_until)] locked_until: Option<DateTime<Utc>>, tenant: String, trace: Option<String>, order_id: i64, } /// A job and its note, read from the queue table by the default fetch. #[derive(Debug, Clone, Inbox, sqlx::FromRow)] struct OrderJob { #[field(headers)] #[sqlx(flatten)] headers: OrderHeaders, note: Option<String>, } // The header map is built from `OrderHeaders` on its first read, here by `Headers<Tenant>`. #[subscriber(InboxQueue::<OrderJob>::new("packing"))] async fn pack(job: &OrderJob, Headers(tenant): Headers<Tenant>) -> HandlerOutcome { tracing::info!( tenant = %tenant.tenant, order = job.headers.order_id, note = ?job.note, "packing" ); HandlerOutcome::ack() } examples/manual/sqlx_headers_layout.rs use ruststream::HeaderMap; use ruststream::runtime::SoloCarried; use ruststream_sqlx::dialect::Column; use ruststream_sqlx::spec::{self, Attempt, Lease}; use ruststream_sqlx::{AttemptRow, HeaderFields, InboxSpec, InboxTable, put_header}; #[derive(Debug, Clone, sqlx::FromRow, JsonSchema)] #[schemars(crate = "ruststream::schemars")] struct OrderHeaders { job_id: i64, attempt: i16, tenant: String, trace: Option<String>, order_id: i64, } #[derive(Debug, Clone, sqlx::FromRow, JsonSchema)] #[schemars(crate = "ruststream::schemars")] struct OrderJob { #[sqlx(flatten)] headers: OrderHeaders, note: Option<String>, } impl InboxTable for OrderJob { type Id = i64; type Table = InboxSpec<(Lease<DateTime<Utc>>, Attempt, spec::HeaderFields)>; const TABLE: Self::Table = InboxSpec::new("order_jobs", Column::new("job_id").generated()) .lease(Column::new("locked_until")) .attempt(Column::new("attempt").generated()) .data(&[ Column::new("tenant"), Column::new("trace"), Column::new("order_id"), ]) .fetching(&[Column::new("note")]) .header_fields(); fn id(&self) -> &i64 { &self.headers.job_id } } impl Input for OrderJob { type Axis = SoloCarried<Self>; } impl AttemptRow for OrderJob { type Attempt = i16; fn attempt(&self) -> &i16 { &self.headers.attempt } } impl HeaderFields for OrderJob { const NAMES: &'static [&'static str] = &["tenant", "trace", "order_id"]; fn header_map(&self) -> HeaderMap { let mut headers = HeaderMap::with_capacity(Self::NAMES.len()); put_header(&mut headers, "tenant", &self.headers.tenant); put_header(&mut headers, "trace", &self.headers.trace); put_header(&mut headers, "order_id", &self.headers.order_id); headers } } struct Packer; impl Handle<OrderJob> for Packer { fn handle( &self, job: &OrderJob, _outs: &(), ctx: &mut Context<'_>, ) -> impl Future<Output = Result<(), HandlerOutcome>> { // The header map is built from the fields on its first read. let tenant = ctx.headers().get_str("tenant").unwrap_or_default(); tracing::info!(tenant, order = job.headers.order_id, note = ?job.note, "packing"); ready(Ok(())) } }

A table with a payload column is in payload mode: the claim lends the column's bytes to the codec, and the handler takes the decoded message. #[field(payload)] marks the column, by hand .payload(..) with PayloadRow, which names the column's type and lends its bytes. A claim reads the row, and the delivery lends those bytes to the codec as they are, with no copy. The codec is the mount's: JSON by default, or any codec of the core the router or the scope names. The bytes are the service's own: binary and empty payloads reach the handler byte for byte, and a publish through a route writes them as the codec encoded them. A row whose bytes do not decode into the handler's type is settled by the subscription's decode policy before the handler runs. A handler that takes a row instead of a message mounts only on a table in row mode.

A signup queue in payload mode: the handler takes the decoded Signup, and the acknowledged row keeps the bytes it was decoded from. Macros Manual examples/sqlx_messages_payload.rs #[derive(Inbox, sqlx::FromRow)] #[inbox(table = "event_jobs")] struct EventJob { #[field(id, generated)] id: i64, #[field(processed_at)] processed_at: Option<DateTime<Utc>>, #[field(locked_until)] locked_until: Option<DateTime<Utc>>, // The message bytes, decoded by the codec of the mount: JSON unless it names another. #[field(payload)] payload: Vec<u8>, } #[subscriber(InboxQueue::<EventJob>::new("signups"))] async fn welcome(signup: &Signup) -> HandlerOutcome { tracing::info!(email = %signup.email, "welcoming"); HandlerOutcome::ack() } examples/manual/sqlx_messages_payload.rs #[derive(sqlx::FromRow)] struct EventJob { id: i64, payload: Vec<u8>, } impl InboxTable for EventJob { type Id = i64; type Table = InboxSpec<(ProcessedAt<DateTime<Utc>>, Lease<DateTime<Utc>>, Payload)>; const TABLE: Self::Table = InboxSpec::new("event_jobs", Column::new("id").generated()) .processed_at(Column::new("processed_at")) .lease(Column::new("locked_until")) .payload(Column::new("payload")); fn id(&self) -> &i64 { &self.id } } // The message bytes, lent to the codec of the mount: JSON unless it names another. impl PayloadRow for EventJob { type Column = Vec<u8>; fn payload(&self) -> &[u8] { &self.payload } } struct Welcome; impl Handle<Signup> for Welcome { fn handle( &self, signup: &Signup, _outs: &(), _ctx: &mut Context<'_>, ) -> impl Future<Output = Result<(), HandlerOutcome>> { tracing::info!(email = %signup.email, "welcoming"); ready(Ok(())) } }

A claimed row that does not decode is settled by the subscription's decode policy before the handler runs, and still spends its attempt. A row decodes in two steps: the driver reads its columns into the struct, and in payload mode the codec reads the payload into the handler's type. A failure at either step reaches the subscription's on_failure(decode = ..) policy, set with FailurePolicies::with_decode. The policy settles the row, and the subscription goes on with the next one. The default policy drops the row: it is deleted, or marked where the table has processed_at. A policy that retries it keeps the row in the table, after a delay with FailurePolicy::RetryAfter. Such a row still reports its attempt: the claim reads the attempt column alone, so max_attempts(n) spends it like any other row, and a retrying policy keeps it only up to the cap. When the attempt column itself does not decode, the row reports no attempt. A claimed id that the service's own fetch returned no row for settles the same way. A row whose id does not decode fails the claim, and every claim that reaches it fails the same way until the row is fixed; the error names the subscription and the table.

A row that does not decode stays in the table and comes back every ten minutes, until a release that reads it ships. Macros Manual examples/sqlx_messages_decoding.rs /// The service on the database `url` names. fn service(url: &str) -> RustStream { let schema_url = url.to_owned(); // Nothing connects here: the broker builds its pool when the service starts. let broker = SqlxBroker::from_url(url, SqlitePoolOptions::new()); // A row that does not decode stays in the table and comes back every ten minutes, until a // release that reads it ships. let keep = FailurePolicy::RetryAfter(Duration::from_secs(600)); RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("mailer", "0.1.0")) // The table, created before the subscription checks it. .on_startup(async move |()| { let mut conn = SqliteConnection::connect(&schema_url).await?; sqlx::raw_sql(SCHEMA).execute(&mut conn).await?; conn.close().await }) .with_broker(broker.route::<SendEmail>("emails"), |b| { b.include(send.on_failure(FailurePolicies::default().with_decode(keep))); }) } examples/manual/sqlx_messages_decoding.rs /// The service on the database `url` names. fn service(url: &str) -> RustStream { let schema_url = url.to_owned(); // Nothing connects here: the broker builds its pool when the service starts. let broker = SqlxBroker::from_url(url, SqlitePoolOptions::new()); // A row that does not decode stays in the table and comes back every ten minutes, until a // release that reads it ships. let keep = FailurePolicy::RetryAfter(Duration::from_secs(600)); RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("mailer", "0.1.0")) // The table, created before the subscription checks it. .on_startup(async move |()| { let mut conn = SqliteConnection::connect(&schema_url).await?; sqlx::raw_sql(SCHEMA).execute(&mut conn).await?; conn.close().await }) .with_broker(broker.route::<SendEmail>("emails"), |b| { let send = subscriber("emails", Sender) .map_source(|_| InboxQueue::<SendEmail>::new("emails")) .on_failure(FailurePolicies::default().with_decode(keep)); b.include(send.build()); }) }

A table without a payload column is in row mode: a handler takes the struct itself as the driver read it, one row or a slice per claim. A struct without a #[field(payload)] field, or a description without .payload(..), is in row mode. Its handler takes &Row, lent by the delivery with no codec and no copy. A batch handler takes &[Row], the rows of one claim in claim order, as a RowBatch. The struct derives Clone, because the test harness keeps a copy of each value, and does not derive Deserialize: a type that deserializes rides the codec. Either mistake is a compile error. Every form serves row mode, and so does transactional mode, where the handler takes &Row beside Ctx<keys::Tx<DB>>. A handler of one row mounts in every form the core offers, a reply and Out slots included; a batch handler of rows mounts in the plain form. The column types are the service's to get right, and a row the driver cannot read settles by the decode policy. A nullable column takes Option<T>. The headers column becomes the delivery's headers, and the row the handler reads holds that column empty. By hand, the description leaves .payload(..) out, names its own columns with .data(..), and the struct writes one line of the core's: impl Input for Row { type Axis = SoloCarried<Self>; }. A row-mode task is written with insert or a Publish of the service's own. In a test, with_value(&row) compares the row a handler took, and received_values::<Row>() returns every row the subscription lent.

The mail queue has no payload column: the handler takes the Mail row, its recipient and subject read as columns. Macros Manual examples/sqlx_messages_rows.rs /// One mail to send: the table has no payload column, so the handler takes the row. #[derive(Debug, Clone, Inbox, sqlx::FromRow)] #[inbox(table = "mail_jobs")] struct Mail { #[field(id, generated)] id: i64, #[field(attempt, generated)] attempt: i16, #[field(locked_until)] locked_until: Option<DateTime<Utc>>, recipient: String, subject: Option<String>, } #[subscriber(InboxQueue::<Mail>::new("mail"))] async fn send(mail: &Mail) -> HandlerOutcome { tracing::info!(to = %mail.recipient, subject = ?mail.subject, mail.attempt, "sending"); HandlerOutcome::ack() } examples/manual/sqlx_messages_rows.rs use ruststream::runtime::SoloCarried; use ruststream_sqlx::dialect::Column; use ruststream_sqlx::spec::{Attempt, Lease}; use ruststream_sqlx::{AttemptRow, InboxSpec, InboxTable}; #[derive(Debug, Clone, sqlx::FromRow, JsonSchema)] #[schemars(crate = "ruststream::schemars")] struct Mail { id: i64, attempt: i16, recipient: String, subject: Option<String>, } impl InboxTable for Mail { type Id = i64; type Table = InboxSpec<(Attempt, Lease<DateTime<Utc>>)>; const TABLE: Self::Table = InboxSpec::new("mail_jobs", Column::new("id").generated()) .attempt(Column::new("attempt").generated()) .lease(Column::new("locked_until")) .data(&[Column::new("recipient"), Column::new("subject")]); fn id(&self) -> &i64 { &self.id } } // Row mode: a handler takes the row itself. impl Input for Mail { type Axis = SoloCarried<Self>; } impl AttemptRow for Mail { type Attempt = i16; fn attempt(&self) -> &i16 { &self.attempt } } struct Sender; impl Handle<Mail> for Sender { fn handle( &self, mail: &Mail, _outs: &(), _ctx: &mut Context<'_>, ) -> impl Future<Output = Result<(), HandlerOutcome>> { tracing::info!(to = %mail.recipient, subject = ?mail.subject, mail.attempt, "sending"); ready(Ok(())) } }

The outbox records each message a service publishes under a registered name until a consumer processed it, and publishes the rest again at startup. The outbox is a plugin over any RustStream broker and needs no broker of its own. The outbox feature turns it on, beside a driver feature: postgres, mysql, sqlite or any. It is independent of the inbox, and a service may enable both. A tracked message goes through four steps. The publish middleware writes a record of the message, then sends it with the record's id in the x-ruststream-outbox-id header. The subscription middleware takes a delivery that carries an id into work by that id, and runs the handler. The handler's outcome then settles the record: an acknowledgement marks it processed. At startup the republish sends every unprocessed record again. A message under a name the registry does not hold passes both middlewares after a comparison of names. A message is delivered at least once. The record is written before the message is sent, so a send that fails, a consumer that stops before its handler finishes, or a handler that asks for the message again leaves the record unprocessed for the next startup. A copy whose record is processed already is acknowledged without running the handler. Two instances of a service that start together may both send the same record again, so a consumer that must not process a message twice checks that itself. A message whose name is not registered costs one comparison per registered name: no allocation and no database call. A tracked publish takes a connection for the record's insert and allocates the id header's value. A tracked delivery takes a connection for the fetch, returns it before the handler runs, and takes one again for the settlement. Under sqlx's default test_before_acquire, each acquire pings the connection first; a pool built with test_before_acquire(false) skips that round trip. The default retry takes no connection, and the republish allocates its body once per startup. The repository's examples/outbox runs the same flow over Redis Pub/Sub, with migrations and a fetch of its own.

The service answers a request on checkout with an OrderPlaced on orders, a registered name: the reply is recorded before it is sent, the acknowledgement of fulfil marks the record, and the startup sends what no consumer processed. RUSTSTREAM_SQLX_OUTBOX=on cargo run -p ruststream-sqlx --example sqlx_outbox --features outbox,sqlite,testing starts it; the switch is there because testing is among the example's features. Macros Manual examples/sqlx_outbox.rs use ruststream::memory::prelude::*; use ruststream_sqlx::{Outbox, outbox}; use sqlx::SqlitePool; /// One record of the `outbox` table. #[derive(Outbox, sqlx::FromRow)] #[outbox(table = "outbox")] struct OrderOutbox { #[field(id)] id: i64, #[field(name)] name: String, #[field(payload)] payload: Vec<u8>, #[field(processed_at)] processed_at: Option<DateTime<Utc>>, } /// The service writes the record; the outbox sends its id with the message. impl outbox::Publish<Sqlite> for OrderOutbox { async fn publish(conn: &mut SqliteConnection, msg: &OutgoingMessage<'_>) -> sqlx::Result<i64> { sqlx::query_scalar("INSERT INTO outbox (name, payload) VALUES (?, ?) RETURNING id") .bind(msg.name()) .bind(msg.payload()) .fetch_one(conn) .await } } /// The reply to `orders` is recorded before it is sent. #[subscriber("checkout", reply)] async fn place(cmd: &PlaceOrder) -> OrderPlaced { OrderPlaced { id: cmd.id } } /// After the acknowledgement, the record is marked processed. #[subscriber("orders")] async fn fulfil(order: &OrderPlaced) -> HandlerOutcome { tracing::info!(order = order.id, "fulfilling the order"); HandlerOutcome::ack() } fn service(pool: SqlitePool) -> impl App { let tracking = outbox! { pool: pool, "orders" => OrderOutbox }; RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("orders", "0.1.0")) .layer(tracking.layer()) .publish_layer(tracking.publish_layer()) .with_broker(MemoryBroker::new(), |b| { b.include(place).out_reply(Publish); b.include(fulfil); // Once the subscriptions are open, the unprocessed records are sent again. b.after_startup(Publish, tracking.republish()); }) } #[tokio::main] async fn main() -> Result<(), Box<dyn Error>> { let pool = SqlitePool::connect("sqlite:orders.db?mode=rwc").await?; sqlx::raw_sql(SCHEMA).execute(&pool).await?; service(pool.clone()).run().await?; pool.close().await; Ok(()) } examples/manual/sqlx_outbox.rs use ruststream::memory::prelude::*; use ruststream_sqlx::outbox::{self, Outbox, OutboxSpec, OutboxTable, TrackedName}; use sqlx::SqlitePool; /// One record of the `outbox` table: the struct holds what the outbox reads. #[derive(sqlx::FromRow)] struct OrderOutbox { id: i64, name: String, payload: Vec<u8>, } impl OutboxTable for OrderOutbox { type Id = i64; type Table = OutboxSpec<(ProcessedAt,)>; const TABLE: Self::Table = OutboxSpec::new( "outbox", Column::new("id"), Column::new("name"), Column::new("payload"), ) .processed_at(Column::new("processed_at")); fn id(&self) -> &i64 { &self.id } fn name(&self) -> &str { &self.name } fn payload(&self) -> &[u8] { &self.payload } } /// The service writes the record; the outbox sends its id with the message. impl outbox::Publish<Sqlite> for OrderOutbox { async fn publish(conn: &mut SqliteConnection, msg: &OutgoingMessage<'_>) -> sqlx::Result<i64> { sqlx::query_scalar("INSERT INTO outbox (name, payload) VALUES (?, ?) RETURNING id") .bind(msg.name()) .bind(msg.payload()) .fetch_one(conn) .await } } /// The name `OrderPlaced` is published under. struct Orders; impl TrackedName for Orders { const NAME: &'static str = "orders"; } /// The reply to `orders` is recorded before it is sent. struct Place; impl Handle<PlaceOrder, OrderPlaced> for Place { fn handle( &self, cmd: &PlaceOrder, _outs: &(), _ctx: &mut Context<'_>, ) -> impl Future<Output = Result<OrderPlaced, HandlerOutcome>> { ready(Ok(OrderPlaced { id: cmd.id })) } } /// After the acknowledgement, the record is marked processed. struct Fulfil; impl Handle<OrderPlaced> for Fulfil { fn handle( &self, order: &OrderPlaced, _outs: &(), _ctx: &mut Context<'_>, ) -> impl Future<Output = Result<(), HandlerOutcome>> { tracing::info!(order = order.id, "fulfilling the order"); ready(Ok(())) } } fn service(pool: SqlitePool) -> impl App { let tracking = Outbox::new(pool).track::<OrderOutbox, Orders>(); RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("orders", "0.1.0")) .layer(tracking.layer()) .publish_layer(tracking.publish_layer()) .with_broker(MemoryBroker::new(), |b| { b.include(subscriber("checkout", Place).reply().build()) .out_reply(Publish); b.include(subscriber("orders", Fulfil).build()); // Once the subscriptions are open, the unprocessed records are sent again. b.after_startup(Publish, tracking.republish()); }) } #[tokio::main] async fn main() -> Result<(), Box<dyn Error>> { let pool = SqlitePool::connect("sqlite:orders.db?mode=rwc").await?; sqlx::raw_sql(SCHEMA).execute(&pool).await?; service(pool.clone()).run().await?; pool.close().await; Ok(()) }

The outbox wraps inbox handlers as any other; a record written from a transactional handler commits on its own, whatever the delivery's outcome. The two middlewares wrap the handlers of an inbox subscription as they wrap the handlers of any broker, and a tracked name may lead into an inbox table. A tracked publish writes its record on a connection of its own, never in the delivery's transaction. So a handler in transactional mode commits its own writes with the delivery, while the record of what it published commits at once: a delivery that is dropped or retried discards the handler's writes and leaves the record. The guarantee stays the outbox's own: the message is delivered at least once, and a consumer that must not process it twice checks that itself. A message tracked into an inbox table carries its record id only where the table keeps headers: a headers column that the table's Publish writes from the message's headers. The consumer's subscription then reads the id back, and its acknowledgement marks the record. A table without a headers column refuses a publish that carries a header, the id among them. SQLite takes one writer at a time, and a transaction holds the write lock from its first write until it ends, or from its start in immediate or exclusive mode. A handler there publishes its tracked messages before its first write through the delivery's transaction: a record's insert on its own connection needs that transaction's write lock, and the transaction waits for the handler. A tracked publish that comes later fails with OutboxError::WriteLockHeld and is not sent. In immediate or exclusive mode it fails at once. After a statement through Tx the record waits for the lock at most the pool's acquire timeout, since SQLite tells whether that statement wrote only by the wait. A record written or marked from a subscription on dedicated threads opens its connection on the app's runtime, so the pool outlives the threads.

take reads an order from order_jobs in transactional mode: it sends a tracked Receipt into receipt_jobs, then writes the order through the delivery's transaction. A dropped order leaves no row in orders, and its receipt is still recorded, delivered and marked. Macros Manual examples/sqlx_outbox_interplay.rs use ruststream_sqlx::prelude::*; use ruststream_sqlx::{Outbox, outbox}; use sqlx::SqlitePool; /// The `headers` column: a JSON object of strings, `NULL` for none. type Headers = Option<Json<BTreeMap<String, String>>>; /// A queue of receipts whose headers column carries the outbox's record id. #[derive(Inbox, sqlx::FromRow)] #[inbox(table = "receipt_jobs")] struct ReceiptJob { #[field(id, generated)] id: i64, #[field(locked_until)] locked_until: Option<DateTime<Utc>>, #[field(headers)] headers: Headers, #[field(payload)] payload: Vec<u8>, } /// The row keeps the message's headers, the record id among them. impl Publish<Sqlite> for ReceiptJob { async fn publish( conn: &mut SqliteConnection, message: &OutgoingMessage<'_>, ) -> Result<(), sqlx::Error> { sqlx::query("INSERT INTO receipt_jobs (headers, payload) VALUES (?, ?)") .bind(Headers::from_headers(message.headers())) .bind(message.payload()) .execute(conn) .await?; Ok(()) } } /// The receipt's record commits on its own; the order's row commits with the delivery. #[subscriber(InboxQueue::<OrderJob>::new("orders"))] async fn take( order: &PlaceOrder, Ctx(mut tx): Ctx<keys::Tx<Sqlite>>, Out(out): Out<impl Publisher>, ) -> HandlerOutcome { if out .message(&Receipt { order: order.id }) .publish() .await .is_err() { return HandlerOutcome::retry(); } let written = sqlx::query("INSERT INTO orders (id) VALUES (?)") .bind(order.id) .execute(&mut *tx) .await; match (written, order.valid) { (Ok(_), true) => HandlerOutcome::ack(), // Dropped: the transaction discards the order's row, and the receipt stays sent. (Ok(_), false) => HandlerOutcome::drop(), (Err(_), _) => HandlerOutcome::retry(), } } /// The acknowledgement marks the receipt's record processed. #[subscriber(InboxQueue::<ReceiptJob>::new("receipts"))] async fn file(receipt: &Receipt) -> HandlerOutcome { tracing::info!(order = receipt.order, "filing the receipt"); HandlerOutcome::ack() } fn service(pool: SqlitePool) -> impl App { let tracking = outbox! { pool: pool.clone(), "receipts" => ReceiptOutbox }; let broker = SqlxBroker::new(pool).route::<OrderJob>("orders"); RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("orders", "0.1.0")) .layer(tracking.layer()) .publish_layer(tracking.publish_layer()) .with_broker(broker, |b| { b.include(take.transactional()) .out(DefaultSlot, Repository::<ReceiptJob>::default()) .build(); b.include(file); b.after_startup(Repository::<ReceiptJob>::default(), tracking.republish()); }) } examples/manual/sqlx_outbox_interplay.rs use ruststream_sqlx::keys::TxContext; use ruststream_sqlx::outbox::Outbox; use ruststream_sqlx::prelude::*; use sqlx::SqlitePool; /// The `headers` column: a JSON object of strings, `NULL` for none. type Headers = Option<Json<BTreeMap<String, String>>>; /// A queue of receipts whose headers column carries the outbox's record id. #[derive(sqlx::FromRow)] struct ReceiptJob { id: i64, headers: Headers, payload: Vec<u8>, } impl InboxTable for ReceiptJob { type Id = i64; type Table = InboxSpec<(Lease<DateTime<Utc>>, HeadersColumn, Payload)>; const TABLE: Self::Table = InboxSpec::new("receipt_jobs", Column::new("id").generated()) .lease(Column::new("locked_until")) .headers(Column::new("headers")) .payload(Column::new("payload")); fn id(&self) -> &i64 { &self.id } } impl HeaderRow for ReceiptJob { type Column = Headers; fn headers_mut(&mut self) -> &mut Headers { &mut self.headers } } impl PayloadRow for ReceiptJob { type Column = Vec<u8>; fn payload(&self) -> &[u8] { &self.payload } } /// The row keeps the message's headers, the record id among them. impl Publish<Sqlite> for ReceiptJob { async fn publish( conn: &mut SqliteConnection, message: &OutgoingMessage<'_>, ) -> Result<(), sqlx::Error> { sqlx::query("INSERT INTO receipt_jobs (headers, payload) VALUES (?, ?)") .bind(Headers::from_headers(message.headers())) .bind(message.payload()) .execute(conn) .await?; Ok(()) } } /// The receipt's record commits on its own; the order's row commits with the delivery. struct Take; // Transactional mode lends the handler the delivery's transaction through its context. impl<Receipts> Handle<PlaceOrder, (), Outs<(Receipts,)>, TxContext<Sqlite>> for Take where Receipts: OutEntry<DefaultSlot, Wire: Publisher>, { async fn handle( &self, order: &PlaceOrder, outs: &Outs<(Receipts,)>, ctx: &mut Context<'_, TxContext<Sqlite>>, ) -> Result<(), HandlerOutcome> { let receipt = Receipt { order: order.id }; if outs .get(DefaultSlot) .message(&receipt) .publish() .await .is_err() { return Err(HandlerOutcome::retry()); } let Ok(Ctx(mut tx)) = Ctx::<keys::Tx<Sqlite>>::from_context(ctx).await; let written = sqlx::query("INSERT INTO orders (id) VALUES (?)") .bind(order.id) .execute(&mut *tx) .await; match (written, order.valid) { (Ok(_), true) => Ok(()), // Dropped: the transaction discards the order's row, and the receipt stays sent. (Ok(_), false) => Err(HandlerOutcome::drop()), (Err(_), _) => Err(HandlerOutcome::retry()), } } } /// The acknowledgement marks the receipt's record processed. struct File; impl Handle<Receipt> for File { fn handle( &self, receipt: &Receipt, _outs: &(), _ctx: &mut Context<'_>, ) -> impl Future<Output = Result<(), HandlerOutcome>> { tracing::info!(order = receipt.order, "filing the receipt"); ready(Ok(())) } } /// The name `Receipt` is published under. struct Receipts; impl TrackedName for Receipts { const NAME: &'static str = "receipts"; } fn service(pool: SqlitePool) -> impl App { let tracking = Outbox::new(pool.clone()).track::<ReceiptOutbox, Receipts>(); let broker = SqlxBroker::new(pool).route::<OrderJob>("orders"); RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("orders", "0.1.0")) .layer(tracking.layer()) .publish_layer(tracking.publish_layer()) .with_broker(broker, |b| { let take = subscriber("orders", Take) .map_source(|_| InboxQueue::<OrderJob>::new("orders")) .transactional(); b.include(take.build()) .out(DefaultSlot, Repository::<ReceiptJob>::default()) .build(); let file = subscriber("receipts", File) .map_source(|_| InboxQueue::<ReceiptJob>::new("receipts")); b.include(file.build()); b.after_startup(Repository::<ReceiptJob>::default(), tracking.republish()); }) }

OutboxError names what the outbox could not do: record a publish, read the unprocessed records, or republish one, a publish with no pool yet, and a record a handler's own SQLite transaction locks out. Each variant names the registered name, and the record type where one is involved: Variant When What follows NoPool a message under a registered name was published before the registry had a pool the message is not sent Record the record's Publish failed; its source is the database's error the message is not sent WriteLockHeld on SQLite, a transactional handler published after its first write through Tx, and its own delivery transaction holds the write lock the record needs (Interplay) the message is not sent Recover the startup republish could not read a name's unprocessed records startup fails Republish the startup republish could not send a record; it names the record's id startup fails A publish through the publish middleware fails with NoPool, Record or WriteLockHeld, as the error of the publisher a handler holds. A publish through wrap fails with TrackedPublishError: Outbox carries the OutboxError, and Publish the wrapped publisher's own error after the record was written, which leaves the record for the next startup. The publish builder wraps either in its own PublishError::Publish. PoolAlreadySet is what a second set_pool returns.

An HTTP endpoint answers each order by what its publish through wrap returned: 202 once the record is written, 503 when it is not, so the client sends the order again. Macros Manual examples/sqlx_outbox_errors.rs use ruststream::runtime::PublishError; use ruststream_sqlx::outbox::TrackedPublishError; /// The status an HTTP endpoint answers an order with. fn status<E: Display>(published: Result<(), PublishError<TrackedPublishError<E>>>) -> u16 { match published { Ok(()) => 202, // Recorded but not sent: the next startup sends it. Err(PublishError::Publish(TrackedPublishError::Publish(error))) => { tracing::warn!(%error, "the order waits for the next startup"); 202 } // Neither recorded nor sent: the client sends the order again. Err(PublishError::Publish(TrackedPublishError::Outbox(error))) => { tracing::warn!(%error, "the order was not recorded"); 503 } Err(error) => { tracing::error!(%error, "the order was not published"); 500 } } } async fn serve(pool: SqlitePool, orders: &[u64]) -> Result<Vec<u16>, Box<dyn Error + Send + Sync>> { let tracking = outbox! { pool: pool, "orders" => OrderOutbox }; let broker = MemoryBroker::new().bindable(); let egress = broker.bind(Publish); let app = RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("orders", "0.1.0")) .publish_layer(tracking.publish_layer()) .with_broker(broker, |_b| {}); let running = app.start().await?; let publisher = tracking.wrap(running.publisher(egress).await?); let mut answers = Vec::with_capacity(orders.len()); for &id in orders { answers.push(status( publisher.message(&OrderPlaced { id }).publish().await, )); } running.shutdown().await?; Ok(answers) } examples/manual/sqlx_outbox_errors.rs use ruststream::runtime::PublishError; use ruststream_sqlx::outbox::TrackedPublishError; /// The status an HTTP endpoint answers an order with. fn status<E: Display>(published: Result<(), PublishError<TrackedPublishError<E>>>) -> u16 { match published { Ok(()) => 202, // Recorded but not sent: the next startup sends it. Err(PublishError::Publish(TrackedPublishError::Publish(error))) => { tracing::warn!(%error, "the order waits for the next startup"); 202 } // Neither recorded nor sent: the client sends the order again. Err(PublishError::Publish(TrackedPublishError::Outbox(error))) => { tracing::warn!(%error, "the order was not recorded"); 503 } Err(error) => { tracing::error!(%error, "the order was not published"); 500 } } } async fn serve(pool: SqlitePool, orders: &[u64]) -> Result<Vec<u16>, Box<dyn Error + Send + Sync>> { let tracking = Outbox::new(pool).track::<OrderOutbox, Orders>(); let broker = MemoryBroker::new().bindable(); let egress = broker.bind(Publish); let app = RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("orders", "0.1.0")) .publish_layer(tracking.publish_layer()) .with_broker(broker, |_b| {}); let running = app.start().await?; let publisher = tracking.wrap(running.publisher(egress).await?); let mut answers = Vec::with_capacity(orders.len()); for &id in orders { answers.push(status( publisher.message(&OrderPlaced { id }).publish().await, )); } running.shutdown().await?; Ok(answers) }

#[derive(Outbox)] describes the outbox table: id, name and payload are required, headers and processed_at optional; the service writes the record. #[outbox(table = "..")] names the table and is required; schema = ".." places it in a schema. #[field(..)] gives a field one role: id: the record's identity. A tracked message carries it in the id header through its Display and FromStr, so an integer and a UUID both fit. name: the name the message was published under. payload: the published bytes. headers: the published headers, a HeaderColumn type such as Option<Json<BTreeMap<String, String>>> (feature json). A republish sends them again. processed_at: the mark of a processed record. The outbox writes it from the database's clock, so any time type fits. A record without it is deleted once processed. Every other field is a plain column sqlx reads, and sqlx's rename, rename_all and skip name the columns. The service writes the record itself, in outbox::Publish, because its statement decides how the name, the payload and the headers are laid out. publish runs on a connection of its own and returns the new record's id. The registry builds the other events from the description and the database's built-in dialect when the record type is registered; Statements replaces them with the service's own. The crate implements OutboxRow for every such record, and a service names it only as a bound. A record described by hand implements OutboxTable with an OutboxSpec chain. OutboxSpec::new takes the table and its three required columns, and type Table lists the typed settings in the order the chain sets them: Headers, ProcessedAt and the events of spec::own. A record with Headers implements HeaderRow for the field that holds the column. Both forms describe one table, and the registry builds the same statements from either. A struct the outbox cannot read does not compile, and the error points at the struct, the field or the word that causes it: no id, name or payload, a role played twice, a column named twice, an unknown role or event, a dot in table or schema. A table whose identifier is longer than the database takes panics when the record type is registered.

OrderOutbox keeps every role, and its Publish stores the headers the message carried; the service stamps each order with its tenant on the way out. Macros Manual examples/sqlx_outbox_record.rs use ruststream_sqlx::{Outbox, outbox}; /// The `headers` column: a JSON object of strings, `NULL` for none. type Headers = Option<Json<BTreeMap<String, String>>>; /// One record of `order_outbox`. #[derive(Outbox, sqlx::FromRow)] #[outbox(table = "order_outbox")] struct OrderOutbox { #[field(id)] id: i64, #[field(name)] name: String, #[field(payload)] payload: Vec<u8>, #[field(headers)] headers: Headers, #[field(processed_at)] processed_at: Option<DateTime<Utc>>, } /// The record keeps what the message carried, so a republish sends the same headers again. impl outbox::Publish<Sqlite> for OrderOutbox { async fn publish(conn: &mut SqliteConnection, msg: &OutgoingMessage<'_>) -> sqlx::Result<i64> { sqlx::query_scalar( "INSERT INTO order_outbox (name, payload, headers) VALUES (?, ?, ?) RETURNING id", ) .bind(msg.name()) .bind(msg.payload()) .bind(Headers::from_headers(msg.headers())) .fetch_one(conn) .await } } examples/manual/sqlx_outbox_record.rs use ruststream_sqlx::outbox::{self, Outbox, OutboxSpec, OutboxTable, TrackedName}; /// The `headers` column: a JSON object of strings, `NULL` for none. type Headers = Option<Json<BTreeMap<String, String>>>; /// One record of `order_outbox`: the struct holds what the outbox reads. #[derive(sqlx::FromRow)] struct OrderOutbox { id: i64, name: String, payload: Vec<u8>, headers: Headers, } impl OutboxTable for OrderOutbox { type Id = i64; type Table = OutboxSpec<(HeadersColumn, ProcessedAt)>; const TABLE: Self::Table = OutboxSpec::new( "order_outbox", Column::new("id"), Column::new("name"), Column::new("payload"), ) .headers(Column::new("headers")) .processed_at(Column::new("processed_at")); fn id(&self) -> &i64 { &self.id } fn name(&self) -> &str { &self.name } fn payload(&self) -> &[u8] { &self.payload } } /// The field that holds the headers column. impl HeaderRow for OrderOutbox { type Column = Headers; fn headers_mut(&mut self) -> &mut Headers { &mut self.headers } } /// The record keeps what the message carried, so a republish sends the same headers again. impl outbox::Publish<Sqlite> for OrderOutbox { async fn publish(conn: &mut SqliteConnection, msg: &OutgoingMessage<'_>) -> sqlx::Result<i64> { sqlx::query_scalar( "INSERT INTO order_outbox (name, payload, headers) VALUES (?, ?, ?) RETURNING id", ) .bind(msg.name()) .bind(msg.payload()) .bind(Headers::from_headers(msg.headers())) .fetch_one(conn) .await } } /// The name `OrderPlaced` is published under. struct Orders; impl TrackedName for Orders { const NAME: &'static str = "orders"; }

outbox! registers record types under the names they track and returns the registry; a name written twice does not compile. The registry is an Outbox: the pool its records live in and the list of names it tracks, each with its record type. outbox! { pool: pool, "orders" => OrderOutbox } builds one on a pool, and without pool: it starts without one, for the set_pool shape. Each registration builds the record's default statements once, from its table's description and the database's built-in dialect. The registry is cheap to clone, and every clone reads the same pool and the same names. It hands out the two middlewares, the republish and wrap. One record type may track several names, so one table serves them all. Each registration republishes only the records of its own name. A name has one record type. By hand, Outbox::new takes the pool and Outbox::deferred starts without one. track::<Record, Name>() registers a record type under a name that is a type, a TrackedName, and a name tracked twice stops the build. register::<Record>(name) takes the name as a &'static str, for a name the service computes, and panics on a repeated name when the app is built. The registry's type lists every record type it holds, so a handle carries no lookup table and an unregistered name costs only the comparisons.

OrderOutbox tracks both orders and refunds: the replies of place and cancel are recorded in the one outbox table, each under its own name. Macros Manual examples/sqlx_outbox_registry.rs use ruststream_sqlx::outbox; fn service(pool: SqlitePool) -> impl App { // Each name has one record type; a name written twice does not compile. let tracking = outbox! { pool: pool, "orders" => OrderOutbox, "refunds" => OrderOutbox, }; RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("orders", "0.1.0")) .layer(tracking.layer()) .publish_layer(tracking.publish_layer()) .with_broker(MemoryBroker::new(), |b| { b.include(place).out_reply(Publish); b.include(cancel).out_reply(Publish); b.include(fulfil); b.include(pay_back); b.after_startup(Publish, tracking.republish()); }) } examples/manual/sqlx_outbox_registry.rs use ruststream_sqlx::outbox::{Outbox, TrackedName}; /// The name `OrderPlaced` is published under. struct Orders; impl TrackedName for Orders { const NAME: &'static str = "orders"; } /// The name `RefundDue` is published under. struct Refunds; impl TrackedName for Refunds { const NAME: &'static str = "refunds"; } fn service(pool: SqlitePool) -> impl App { // Each name has one record type; a name tracked twice stops the build. let tracking = Outbox::new(pool) .track::<OrderOutbox, Orders>() .track::<OrderOutbox, Refunds>(); RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("orders", "0.1.0")) .layer(tracking.layer()) .publish_layer(tracking.publish_layer()) .with_broker(MemoryBroker::new(), |b| { b.include(subscriber("checkout", Place).reply().build()) .out_reply(Publish); b.include(subscriber("cancellations", Cancel).reply().build()) .out_reply(Publish); b.include(subscriber("orders", Fulfil).build()); b.include(subscriber("refunds", PayBack).build()); b.after_startup(Publish, tracking.republish()); }) }

b.after_startup(policy, tracking.republish()) sends every unprocessed record again once the subscriptions are open; republish_names picks names. Outbox::republish returns a Republishing, the hook after_startup runs with the broker's live publisher of the policy it names. For each registered name it reads the unprocessed records through the record's Recover event and publishes each one with its id, its payload and the headers its record kept. A consumer then takes each copy as any tracked delivery, so a copy whose record a consumer processed in the meantime is acknowledged without its handler. The hook runs once the subscriptions are open, so a consumer in the same service receives what its own service sent before a restart. republish_names republishes only the names it lists, for a service whose names live on several brokers: each broker's after_startup republishes the names that broker carries. A name it lists that the registry does not hold panics when the app is built. A record the republish cannot read fails startup with OutboxError::Recover, and one it cannot send with OutboxError::Republish. A service whose records stay with a selection of its own writes Recover itself. The republish allocates its body once per startup.

The broker's after_startup republishes the unprocessed records of orders through its Publish policy; fulfil consumes them and marks each record. Macros Manual examples/sqlx_outbox_republish.rs use ruststream::memory::prelude::*; use ruststream_sqlx::outbox; use sqlx::SqlitePool; fn service(pool: SqlitePool) -> impl App { let tracking = outbox! { pool: pool, "orders" => OrderOutbox }; RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("orders", "0.1.0")) .layer(tracking.layer()) .publish_layer(tracking.publish_layer()) .with_broker(MemoryBroker::new(), |b| { b.include(place).out_reply(Publish); b.include(fulfil); // Runs once the subscriptions are open, through this broker's publisher. b.after_startup(Publish, tracking.republish()); }) } examples/manual/sqlx_outbox_republish.rs use ruststream::memory::prelude::*; use ruststream_sqlx::outbox::Outbox; use sqlx::SqlitePool; fn service(pool: SqlitePool) -> impl App { let tracking = Outbox::new(pool).track::<OrderOutbox, Orders>(); RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("orders", "0.1.0")) .layer(tracking.layer()) .publish_layer(tracking.publish_layer()) .with_broker(MemoryBroker::new(), |b| { b.include(subscriber("checkout", Place).reply().build()) .out_reply(Publish); b.include(subscriber("orders", Fulfil).build()); // Runs once the subscriptions are open, through this broker's publisher. b.after_startup(Publish, tracking.republish()); }) }

Inside #[ruststream::app] the registry starts without a pool, and on_startup builds one and hands it over with set_pool; the service closes it. #[ruststream::app] builds the app before the Tokio runtime exists, and sqlx builds a pool only inside one. So the registry starts without a pool: outbox! without pool:, or Outbox::deferred by hand. on_startup runs inside the runtime, builds the pool and hands it to a clone of the registry with set_pool. Every handle the registry gave out, the middlewares and the republish among them, reads that one pool. An app built inside a runtime passes the pool directly instead: outbox! { pool: pool, .. } or Outbox::new. set_pool takes one pool, once: a second call, or a call on a registry built with a pool, returns PoolAlreadySet. Until the pool is set, a tracked publish fails with OutboxError::NoPool, which names the name, and a tracked delivery is retried without its handler. The value on_startup returns becomes the app's state, and after_shutdown receives it: the service closes the pool there, once the handlers have finished and the brokers have stopped.

service builds the app from a database URL, and #[ruststream::app] runs it on the service's own file. Macros Manual examples/sqlx_outbox_pool.rs use std::convert::Infallible; use std::io; use ruststream::memory::prelude::*; use ruststream_sqlx::outbox; use sqlx::SqlitePool; fn service(url: String) -> impl App { // No pool yet: the Tokio runtime starts after this builder, and sqlx builds a pool only there. let tracking = outbox! { "orders" => OrderOutbox }; let registry = tracking.clone(); RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("orders", "0.1.0")) .on_startup(async move |()| { let pool = SqlitePool::connect(&url).await.map_err(io::Error::other)?; // Every handle the registry gave out reads this one pool. registry.set_pool(pool.clone()).map_err(io::Error::other)?; Ok::<_, io::Error>(pool) }) .layer(tracking.layer()) .publish_layer(tracking.publish_layer()) // Runs once the handlers have finished and the brokers have stopped. .after_shutdown(async move |pool| { pool.close().await; Ok::<_, Infallible>(()) }) .with_broker(MemoryBroker::new(), |b| { b.include(place).out_reply(Publish); b.include(fulfil); b.after_startup(Publish, tracking.republish()); }) } #[ruststream::app] fn app() -> impl App { service("sqlite:orders.db".to_owned()) } examples/manual/sqlx_outbox_pool.rs use std::convert::Infallible; use std::io; use ruststream::memory::prelude::*; use ruststream_sqlx::outbox::Outbox; use sqlx::SqlitePool; fn service(url: String) -> impl App { // No pool yet: the Tokio runtime starts after this builder, and sqlx builds a pool only there. let tracking = Outbox::deferred().track::<OrderOutbox, Orders>(); let registry = tracking.clone(); RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("orders", "0.1.0")) .on_startup(async move |()| { let pool = SqlitePool::connect(&url).await.map_err(io::Error::other)?; // Every handle the registry gave out reads this one pool. registry.set_pool(pool.clone()).map_err(io::Error::other)?; Ok::<_, io::Error>(pool) }) .layer(tracking.layer()) .publish_layer(tracking.publish_layer()) // Runs once the handlers have finished and the brokers have stopped. .after_shutdown(async move |pool| { pool.close().await; Ok::<_, Infallible>(()) }) .with_broker(MemoryBroker::new(), |b| { b.include(subscriber("checkout", Place).reply().build()) .out_reply(Publish); b.include(subscriber("orders", Fulfil).build()); b.after_startup(Publish, tracking.republish()); }) } #[ruststream::app] fn app() -> impl App { service("sqlite:orders.db".to_owned()) }

#[outbox(custom(fetch, ack, retry, discard, recover))] replaces a record's default statement with the service's own, for a status of its own or a saga. Each event is a trait of its own, and the registry runs the record's impl in place of the default: Event Trait Default a delivery takes the record into work Fetch reads the record while it is unprocessed the handler acknowledged Ack marks the record processed the handler asked again Retry runs nothing the handler dropped the message Discard marks the record processed the startup republish Recover reads the unprocessed records of one name Fetch returns Option<Self>: None means the record is processed or taken already, and the delivery is acknowledged without its handler. So a fetch of the service's own decides what "taken" means, a stamp, a status column or a lease, and the other events release or finish it. Publish has no default: it is always the service's own and is never listed. A default Retry takes no connection; a Retry of the service's own takes one, as the other events do. By hand, the record's OutboxSpec names each event with .own::<own::Fetch>() and the others, and its type Table lists the same markers of outbox::spec::own. A record type that names an event and lacks its trait does not register, and the error names the missing trait.

OrderOutbox stamps taken_at when a consumer takes the record, and its retry releases the record and counts the attempt; the acknowledgement keeps the default mark. The repository's examples/outbox takes its records with such a fetch on Postgres. Macros Manual examples/sqlx_outbox_statements.rs use ruststream_sqlx::{Outbox, outbox}; use sqlx::{Sqlite, SqliteConnection}; /// One record of `order_outbox`, taken and released by statements of the service's own. #[derive(Outbox, sqlx::FromRow)] #[outbox(table = "order_outbox", custom(fetch, retry))] struct OrderOutbox { #[field(id)] id: i64, #[field(name)] name: String, #[field(payload)] payload: Vec<u8>, #[field(processed_at)] processed_at: Option<DateTime<Utc>>, } impl outbox::Publish<Sqlite> for OrderOutbox { async fn publish(conn: &mut SqliteConnection, msg: &OutgoingMessage<'_>) -> sqlx::Result<i64> { sqlx::query_scalar("INSERT INTO order_outbox (name, payload) VALUES (?, ?) RETURNING id") .bind(msg.name()) .bind(msg.payload()) .fetch_one(conn) .await } } /// Takes the record into work, or finds it taken or processed already (`None`). impl outbox::Fetch<Sqlite> for OrderOutbox { async fn fetch(conn: &mut SqliteConnection, id: &i64) -> sqlx::Result<Option<Self>> { sqlx::query_as( "UPDATE order_outbox SET taken_at = CURRENT_TIMESTAMP WHERE id = ? AND taken_at IS NULL AND processed_at IS NULL RETURNING id, name, payload, processed_at", ) .bind(id) .fetch_optional(conn) .await } } /// Releases a record its consumer asked for again, and counts the attempt. impl outbox::Retry<Sqlite> for OrderOutbox { async fn retry(conn: &mut SqliteConnection, id: &i64) -> sqlx::Result<()> { sqlx::query("UPDATE order_outbox SET taken_at = NULL, attempts = attempts + 1 WHERE id = ?") .bind(id) .execute(conn) .await .map(drop) } } examples/manual/sqlx_outbox_statements.rs use ruststream_sqlx::dialect::Column; use ruststream_sqlx::outbox::spec::{ProcessedAt, own}; use ruststream_sqlx::outbox::{self, OutboxSpec, OutboxTable}; use sqlx::{Sqlite, SqliteConnection}; /// One record of `order_outbox`, taken and released by statements of the service's own. #[derive(sqlx::FromRow)] struct OrderOutbox { id: i64, name: String, payload: Vec<u8>, } impl OutboxTable for OrderOutbox { type Id = i64; type Table = OutboxSpec<(ProcessedAt, own::Fetch, own::Retry)>; const TABLE: Self::Table = OutboxSpec::new( "order_outbox", Column::new("id"), Column::new("name"), Column::new("payload"), ) .processed_at(Column::new("processed_at")) .own::<own::Fetch>() .own::<own::Retry>(); fn id(&self) -> &i64 { &self.id } fn name(&self) -> &str { &self.name } fn payload(&self) -> &[u8] { &self.payload } } impl outbox::Publish<Sqlite> for OrderOutbox { async fn publish(conn: &mut SqliteConnection, msg: &OutgoingMessage<'_>) -> sqlx::Result<i64> { sqlx::query_scalar("INSERT INTO order_outbox (name, payload) VALUES (?, ?) RETURNING id") .bind(msg.name()) .bind(msg.payload()) .fetch_one(conn) .await } } /// Takes the record into work, or finds it taken or processed already (`None`). impl outbox::Fetch<Sqlite> for OrderOutbox { async fn fetch(conn: &mut SqliteConnection, id: &i64) -> sqlx::Result<Option<Self>> { sqlx::query_as( "UPDATE order_outbox SET taken_at = CURRENT_TIMESTAMP WHERE id = ? AND taken_at IS NULL AND processed_at IS NULL RETURNING id, name, payload", ) .bind(id) .fetch_optional(conn) .await } } /// Releases a record its consumer asked for again, and counts the attempt. impl outbox::Retry<Sqlite> for OrderOutbox { async fn retry(conn: &mut SqliteConnection, id: &i64) -> sqlx::Result<()> { sqlx::query("UPDATE order_outbox SET taken_at = NULL, attempts = attempts + 1 WHERE id = ?") .bind(id) .execute(conn) .await .map(drop) } }

A test build leaves the outbox off, so a test needs no outbox table; RUSTSTREAM_SQLX_OUTBOX=on turns it on for the whole test process. A build with the testing feature leaves the outbox off: the two middlewares pass every message untouched, wrap sends straight to the publisher it wraps, and the republish sends nothing. A test of the handlers then runs on the service's production app with no outbox table and no database for it. A production build always tracks, and the switch is compiled out. RUSTSTREAM_SQLX_OUTBOX=on in the environment turns the outbox on in a test build, and any other value leaves it off. The variable is read once per process, the first time the outbox runs, and tests share one process, so it is set outside them: in a just recipe, a CI job or a nextest profile. A test of tracking itself runs only with the switch on and returns early without it; a job that sets RUSTSTREAM_REQUIRE_LIVE then fails such a test instead of passing it. The testing feature also reaches cargo run --example and cargo build --all-targets of a crate that enables it, so an example among the outbox's pages runs with the switch set.

The test drives the service of the Transactional outbox page over a database that has no tables, and runs only without the switch: the order reaches its consumer and carries no record id. Macros Manual examples/sqlx_outbox_switch.rs #[tokio::test(flavor = "multi_thread", worker_threads = 2)] async fn a_test_of_the_handlers_needs_no_outbox_table() -> Result<(), Box<dyn Error>> { // The switch is read once per process: with it on, this process tracks every message. if env::var("RUSTSTREAM_SQLX_OUTBOX").as_deref() == Ok("on") { return Ok(()); } let (pool, _keeper) = database("sqlx_outbox_switch").await?; let tb = TestApp::start(service(pool)).await?; tb.broker::<MemoryBroker>() .message(&PlaceOrder { id: 7 }) .publish() .await?; tb.broker::<MemoryBroker>() .subscriber("orders") .assert_called_once() .with(&OrderPlaced { id: 7 }) .settled(HandlerOutcome::ack()); // Nothing was recorded, so the order carries no record id. let published = tb.broker::<MemoryBroker>().published::<()>("orders"); let ids: Vec<_> = published .messages() .iter() .map(|message| message.headers().get_str(OUTBOX_ID_HEADER)) .collect(); assert_eq!(ids, [None]); Ok(()) } examples/manual/sqlx_outbox_switch.rs #[tokio::test(flavor = "multi_thread", worker_threads = 2)] async fn a_test_of_the_handlers_needs_no_outbox_table() -> Result<(), Box<dyn Error>> { // The switch is read once per process: with it on, this process tracks every message. if env::var("RUSTSTREAM_SQLX_OUTBOX").as_deref() == Ok("on") { return Ok(()); } let (pool, _keeper) = database("manual_sqlx_outbox_switch").await?; let tb = TestApp::start(service(pool)).await?; tb.broker::<MemoryBroker>() .message(&PlaceOrder { id: 7 }) .publish() .await?; tb.broker::<MemoryBroker>() .subscriber("orders") .assert_called_once() .with(&OrderPlaced { id: 7 }) .settled(HandlerOutcome::ack()); // Nothing was recorded, so the order carries no record id. let published = tb.broker::<MemoryBroker>().published::<()>("orders"); let ids: Vec<_> = published .messages() .iter() .map(|message| message.headers().get_str(OUTBOX_ID_HEADER)) .collect(); assert_eq!(ids, [None]); Ok(()) }

Outbox::layer and publish_layer track messages: the publish records then sends, and the delivery's outcome settles its record by its id. publish_layer returns a TrackingPublishLayer, mounted with RustStream::publish_layer. It reaches everything a handler publishes, replies and Out slots alike. A message under a registered name is recorded through the record's Publish, then sent with the record's id in OUTBOX_ID_HEADER. A record that fails is not sent, and the publish fails with OutboxError::Record. layer returns a TrackingLayer, mounted with RustStream::layer. A delivery under a registered name that carries an id is taken into work by the record's fetch, on a connection the layer returns before the handler runs, so the handler can publish tracked messages of its own. The handler's outcome then settles the record: Outcome Event Default statement acknowledged outbox::Ack marks the record processed asked again (retry, retry_after) outbox::Retry none: the record waits for the next startup dropped outbox::Discard marks the record processed A record without processed_at is deleted where the default marks it. A record the fetch finds processed already acknowledges the delivery without running the handler, which is how a copy sent twice reaches its consumer once. A fetch that fails retries the delivery without the handler. A settlement that fails logs a warning and keeps the handler's outcome, and the record stays for the next startup. A delivery without the header, with a header that is not an id, or under a name the registry does not hold runs untracked. Both layers pass a message whose name is not registered after one comparison per registered name.

fulfil acknowledges an order in stock, whose record is marked, and asks again for one out of stock, whose record waits; the subscription takes one attempt, so the broker does not deliver that order again. Macros Manual examples/sqlx_outbox_tracking.rs use ruststream::memory::prelude::*; use ruststream_sqlx::outbox; use sqlx::SqlitePool; #[subscriber("checkout", reply)] async fn place(cmd: &PlaceOrder) -> OrderPlaced { OrderPlaced { id: cmd.id, in_stock: cmd.in_stock, } } /// The outcome settles the record: an acknowledgement marks it, a retry leaves it. #[subscriber("orders")] async fn fulfil(order: &OrderPlaced) -> HandlerOutcome { if order.in_stock { tracing::info!(order = order.id, "fulfilling the order"); HandlerOutcome::ack() } else { HandlerOutcome::retry() } } fn service(pool: SqlitePool) -> impl App { let tracking = outbox! { pool: pool, "orders" => OrderOutbox }; RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("orders", "0.1.0")) // Takes a delivery that carries a record id into work and settles the record. .layer(tracking.layer()) // Records a message under a registered name, then sends it with the record's id. .publish_layer(tracking.publish_layer()) .with_broker(MemoryBroker::new(), |b| { b.include(place).out_reply(Publish); // One attempt: an order out of stock is not delivered again, and its record waits. b.include(fulfil).max_attempts(nonzero!(1u32)); }) } examples/manual/sqlx_outbox_tracking.rs use ruststream::memory::prelude::*; use ruststream_sqlx::outbox::Outbox; use sqlx::SqlitePool; struct Place; impl Handle<PlaceOrder, OrderPlaced> for Place { fn handle( &self, cmd: &PlaceOrder, _outs: &(), _ctx: &mut Context<'_>, ) -> impl Future<Output = Result<OrderPlaced, HandlerOutcome>> { ready(Ok(OrderPlaced { id: cmd.id, in_stock: cmd.in_stock, })) } } /// The outcome settles the record: an acknowledgement marks it, a retry leaves it. struct Fulfil; impl Handle<OrderPlaced> for Fulfil { fn handle( &self, order: &OrderPlaced, _outs: &(), _ctx: &mut Context<'_>, ) -> impl Future<Output = Result<(), HandlerOutcome>> { if order.in_stock { tracing::info!(order = order.id, "fulfilling the order"); ready(Ok(())) } else { ready(Err(HandlerOutcome::retry())) } } } /// The name `OrderPlaced` is published under. struct Orders; impl TrackedName for Orders { const NAME: &'static str = "orders"; } fn service(pool: SqlitePool) -> impl App { let tracking = Outbox::new(pool).track::<OrderOutbox, Orders>(); RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("orders", "0.1.0")) // Takes a delivery that carries a record id into work and settles the record. .layer(tracking.layer()) // Records a message under a registered name, then sends it with the record's id. .publish_layer(tracking.publish_layer()) .with_broker(MemoryBroker::new(), |b| { b.include(subscriber("checkout", Place).reply().build()) .out_reply(Publish); // One attempt: an order out of stock is not delivered again, and its record waits. b.include(subscriber("orders", Fulfil).build()) .max_attempts(nonzero!(1u32)); }) }

Outbox::wrap gives a publisher outside the publish pipeline the same tracking, for an HTTP endpoint or an after_startup hook. The publish pipeline reaches what handlers publish. A publisher from RunningApp::publisher, or the one an after_startup hook receives, runs outside it, so the publish middleware never sees its messages. wrap takes such a publisher and returns a TrackedPublisher, a publisher like any other: a message under a registered name is recorded first, then sent with the record's id. A message under any other name goes straight to the wrapped publisher. A publish through it fails with TrackedPublishError: Outbox when the record was not written and the message was not sent, Publish when the wrapped publisher failed after the record was written. In the second case the record stays unprocessed, and the next startup sends it. The wrapper borrows the payload for the record in whatever form the publisher takes it, so the message is not copied.

The service starts its app by hand, takes the live publisher of a bound Publish policy, as an HTTP server would, and publishes each order through the wrapper. Macros Manual examples/sqlx_outbox_wrap.rs use ruststream::memory::prelude::*; use ruststream_sqlx::outbox; use sqlx::SqlitePool; async fn serve(pool: SqlitePool, orders: &[u64]) -> Result<(), Box<dyn Error + Send + Sync>> { let tracking = outbox! { pool: pool, "orders" => OrderOutbox }; let broker = MemoryBroker::new().bindable(); let egress = broker.bind(Publish); let app = RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("orders", "0.1.0")) .publish_layer(tracking.publish_layer()) .with_broker(broker, |_b| {}); let running = app.start().await?; // The running app's publisher bypasses the publish pipeline; `wrap` gives it the tracking. let publisher = tracking.wrap(running.publisher(egress).await?); for &id in orders { publisher.message(&OrderPlaced { id }).publish().await?; tracing::info!(order = id, "order recorded and sent"); } running.shutdown().await?; Ok(()) } examples/manual/sqlx_outbox_wrap.rs use ruststream::memory::prelude::*; use ruststream_sqlx::outbox::Outbox; use sqlx::SqlitePool; async fn serve(pool: SqlitePool, orders: &[u64]) -> Result<(), Box<dyn Error + Send + Sync>> { let tracking = Outbox::new(pool).track::<OrderOutbox, Orders>(); let broker = MemoryBroker::new().bindable(); let egress = broker.bind(Publish); let app = RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("orders", "0.1.0")) .publish_layer(tracking.publish_layer()) .with_broker(broker, |_b| {}); let running = app.start().await?; // The running app's publisher bypasses the publish pipeline; `wrap` gives it the tracking. let publisher = tracking.wrap(running.publisher(egress).await?); for &id in orders { publisher.message(&OrderPlaced { id }).publish().await?; tracing::info!(order = id, "order recorded and sent"); } running.shutdown().await?; Ok(()) }

A publish writes a row through the row's Publish, the service's own INSERT; Repository names the table at compile time, a static call per publish. Publish<DB> is the statement of a queue table that takes a published message. Its publish(conn, message) receives the message's name, its encoded bytes and its headers, and lays them out in the table's columns. In a table with a group column, the name usually goes there, so a subscription of that group reads the row. The trait has no default: a row without it is not a publisher, and a mount that names it does not compile. Repository::<Row>::default() is the publish policy of Row's table. A mount site names it wherever a registration publishes: .out_reply(Repository::<Job>::default()) for a reply, .out(Slot, Repository::<Job>::default()) for an Out slot. The runtime pairs it with the connected broker at startup into a RepositoryPublisher. A publisher outside a handler, such as an HTTP endpoint's, comes from SqlxBroker::new(pool).bindable(), bind(Repository::<Job>::default()) and running.publisher(..). Each publish takes a connection of the pool, runs the row's Publish on it and commits on its own. A handler's transaction does not cover it: a row that must commit with the handler's writes goes in through Insert on the handler's Tx. A message whose header the table cannot hold byte for byte is refused before the statement runs, with SqlxBrokerError::Header; a headers column holds them. A failed statement returns SqlxBrokerError::Publish, which names the message's name, the table and the row type. After shutdown a publisher answers SqlxBrokerError::Closed. A publish through a repository wakes the subscriptions of its table and group in the same process at once. A name the service does not know at compile time goes through a route instead: the broker's default publisher looks the name up.

An order's confirmation becomes a row of jobs in the group emails, and the second subscription of the service reads it. Macros Manual examples/sqlx_publishing_repository.rs use ruststream::OutgoingMessage; use sqlx::{Sqlite, SqliteConnection}; /// One row of `jobs`: the group column holds the name a message was published to. #[derive(Inbox, sqlx::FromRow)] #[inbox(table = "jobs")] struct Job { #[field(id, generated)] id: i64, #[field(group)] name: String, #[field(locked_until)] locked_until: Option<DateTime<Utc>>, #[field(payload)] payload: Vec<u8>, } /// The service's own insert: the name goes to the group column, the bytes to the payload. impl Publish<Sqlite> for Job { async fn publish( conn: &mut SqliteConnection, message: &OutgoingMessage<'_>, ) -> Result<(), sqlx::Error> { sqlx::query("INSERT INTO jobs (name, payload) VALUES (?, ?)") .bind(message.name()) .bind(message.payload()) .execute(conn) .await?; Ok(()) } } #[subscriber(InboxQueue::<Job>::new("orders"), reply)] async fn confirm(order: &Order) -> Confirmation { Confirmation { order: order.id } } #[subscriber(InboxQueue::<Job>::new("emails"))] async fn email(confirmation: &Confirmation) -> HandlerOutcome { tracing::info!(order = confirmation.order, "emailing the confirmation"); HandlerOutcome::ack() } /// The service on the database `url` names. fn service(url: &str) -> RustStream { let schema_url = url.to_owned(); // Nothing connects here: the broker builds its pool when the service starts. let broker = SqlxBroker::from_url(url, SqlitePoolOptions::new()); RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("orders", "0.1.0")) // The table, created before the subscription checks it. .on_startup(async move |()| { let mut conn = SqliteConnection::connect(&schema_url).await?; sqlx::raw_sql(SCHEMA).execute(&mut conn).await?; conn.close().await }) .with_broker(broker.route::<Job>("orders"), |b| { // The confirmation becomes a row of `jobs` in the group `emails`. b.include(confirm).out_reply(Repository::<Job>::default()); b.include(email); }) } examples/manual/sqlx_publishing_repository.rs use ruststream::OutgoingMessage; use sqlx::{Sqlite, SqliteConnection}; /// One row of `jobs`: the group column holds the name a message was published to. #[derive(sqlx::FromRow)] struct Job { id: i64, payload: Vec<u8>, } impl InboxTable for Job { type Id = i64; Ok(()) } } struct Confirm; impl Handle<Order, Confirmation> for Confirm { fn handle( &self, order: &Order, _outs: &(), _ctx: &mut Context<'_>, ) -> impl Future<Output = Result<Confirmation, HandlerOutcome>> { ready(Ok(Confirmation { order: order.id })) } } struct Email; impl Handle<Confirmation> for Email { fn handle( &self, confirmation: &Confirmation, _outs: &(), _ctx: &mut Context<'_>, ) -> impl Future<Output = Result<(), HandlerOutcome>> { tracing::info!(order = confirmation.order, "emailing the confirmation"); ready(Ok(())) } } /// The service on the database `url` names. fn service(url: &str) -> RustStream { let schema_url = url.to_owned(); // Nothing connects here: the broker builds its pool when the service starts. let broker = SqlxBroker::from_url(url, SqlitePoolOptions::new()); RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("orders", "0.1.0")) // The table, created before the subscription checks it. .on_startup(async move |()| { let mut conn = SqliteConnection::connect(&schema_url).await?; sqlx::raw_sql(SCHEMA).execute(&mut conn).await?; SqlxBroker::route leads a name into a row type's table in both directions; Routed, the default for replies and slots, looks each name up. .route::<Job>("orders") on the broker serves two directions. A publish to orders writes a row of Job's table through the row's Publish. #[subscriber("orders")] opens a subscription by that name on the same table. A name ending in * leads every name that starts with what precedes it: reports.* takes reports.daily and reports.weekly. An exact name wins over a prefix, and a longer prefix over a shorter one. A name routed twice leads to the last row type. Routed is the broker's default publish policy. A reply or an Out slot that names no policy of its own publishes through it, and so does a test's input through the harness. A publish looks its name up in the route table: one hash lookup for an exact name, the prefixes scanned only when none matches, then one dynamic call into the row's Publish. That call's future stays in place in 1024 bytes, so a routed publish allocates what a repository publish does. A row whose Publish future is larger is boxed: one allocation per publish on its route. A name no route leads anywhere fails the publish with SqlxBrokerError::NoRoute, which names the route to add. A route asks of the broker's dialect what an InboxQueue of the row asks: the table's form and the isolation level or SQLite mode the struct declares. A routed publish wakes the subscriptions of its table and group in the same process, as a repository publish does.

The prefix route reports.* leads the daily report a client publishes and the weekly report the service replies with into one table. The reply names no policy, so it goes through the routes. A handler's outcome is a statement on its row: ack deletes it or sets processed_at, retry returns it at once with one more attempt, drop finishes it. What a handler answers decides the row's fate: Outcome The row ack() is deleted, or marked with the current time where the table has a processed_at column retry() returns to the queue at once, and its next delivery reads one more attempt retry_after(d) stays out of the queue until its retry_after comes drop() is finished as an acknowledgement finishes it A row marked with processed_at stays in the table, out of every claim, for an audit or a later cleanup. The statement runs where the form holds the row: in the claim's transaction, by the delivery's lease, or on the session that holds its key. It takes effect together with the end of that hold, so a row and its outcome never part. A settlement whose statement fails reports itself, and the row returns as it would after a crash. max_attempts(n) with dead_letter(..) caps the retries and moves a spent row aside. A table may run its own SQL for an outcome, an acknowledgement that moves the row to a sent group for one (Events); it runs in the transaction the crate commits, as the built-in statement does. An acknowledgement takes the row out of what the claim selects, so a statement of one's own that leaves the row claimable delivers it again.

The mail server greylists a first delivery, so the handler retries it at once; an address that cannot receive mail is dropped, and both end marked in processed_at. max_attempts(n) with dead_letter(..) moves a row whose attempts are spent into another group, or into a table with the same columns. The two steps come together at the mount site, and a mount that declares one without the other stops the service at startup. The cap reads the row's #[field(attempt)] column, which counts the deliveries, the first one included; a cap on a table without it stops startup too. A delivery that fails its n-th attempt moves the row instead of returning it: a table with a group column moves it to the dead_letter group, a table without one into the dead_letter table. A dead-letter table has the same columns as the queue's; on MySQL and MariaDB the move is two statements in one transaction. With max_attempts(1) every failure moves the row at once. A delayed retry obeys the cap too. The dead-letter group is an ordinary queue of the table: an InboxQueue of that name reads it, or an operator reviews it in place. A subscription by name refuses both steps at startup. A table may move its rows with its own SQL instead, through the DeadLetter event (Events).
