retry_after(d) hides the row until its retry_after column comes due; a table without the column returns the row at once and logs a warning. The settlement writes "now" plus d into the row's #[field(retry_after)] column, and the row's next delivery reads one more attempt. A claim takes only rows whose retry_after has come, so the row waits in the table, with no timer in the service and nothing lost if the process stops. The column holds a time type, and "now" comes from the table's clock. A table without the column returns the row at once, and the runtime logs a warning. The backoff is the handler's: it reads the delivery's attempt and answers with the delay it wants. A delayed retry counts against a retry cap as an immediate one does. In a FIFO group the delayed row moves behind the rows due before it. In process the queue reads "now" off the tokio clock, so a test on a paused clock brings the row due with tb.advance(d).

InboxQueue reads one queue of a table: its name selects a group where the table has a group column and addresses the whole table where it has none. InboxQueue::<Row>::new(name) takes the struct that describes the table and the queue's name. The descriptor goes where a name goes, as the first argument of #[subscriber(..)]; the manual form mounts it on subscriber(name, body) with map_source. Two settings belong to the descriptor, and both default to the broker's: the poll interval and, on a lease table, the lease. The mount site adds the rest: workers, batches, transactional mode, dedicated threads and a retry cap. A subscription claims rows when the runtime polls its stream, so it takes rows as fast as its handlers settle them. Every claimed row is delivered at least once: the row of a process that crashed returns to the queue by the rules of its table's form. A broker serves one subscription per queue, and one per table without a group column; a second one stops the service at startup. A retry never copies a row: the claim's own statements move it, so the mount site names no retry publisher. A plain name in #[subscriber("emails")] reads the table its route leads to instead, as Names shows.

A slice handler gets one claim of up to batch(n) rows; each row settles on its own, and in the row lock form the settlements commit together. A handler over &[T] is a batch handler, and batch(n) at the mount site is the most rows one claim takes for it. A claim takes what is due at once and waits for nothing, so a quiet queue yields batches smaller than n. A Vec<HandlerOutcome> settles row i with outcome i, and a single outcome settles them all. A row that does not decode is settled by the decode policy, and the batch keeps its other rows. On SQLite the rows of a batch come in no particular order. Each form settles a batch its own way: Form A batch row lock shares the claim's transaction and one connection; each row settles in it, and the settlements take effect together when the last delivery finishes lease settles each row on its own, on a connection taken for the statement advisory lock holds a connection per row and settles each row on it; it holds one row per key and ends where the pool has no connection to spare In the row lock form a settlement whose statement fails rolls the whole batch back, its rows return, and the later settlements fail with SqlxBrokerError::BatchRolledBack. A table in row mode hands a batch handler &[Row], the rows themselves (Rows). A batch handler runs outside transactional mode: a batch mounted with .transactional() does not compile. In the manual form the body is an impl Handle<[T]>, where Ok(()) acknowledges the batch and Err(outcomes) settles it row by row.

#[field(group, fifo = true)] keeps each group in order: one row of a group in work at a time across every broker, the head first. A FIFO group has at most one row in work, however many brokers and processes read it. Its rows go out in claim order: a smaller priority first, then an earlier retry_after, then the smaller id, each where the table has the column. The group's first unfinished row in that order is its head, and a claim takes the head alone. The rows behind the head wait while it is in work or not yet due. retry() keeps a row at the head, so a change that failed goes again before the ones behind it. retry_after(d) gives the row a later retry_after, and it moves behind the rows due before it; on a table with priority it moves only among the rows of its own priority. A head that keeps failing holds its group back, so a FIFO table pairs with a retry cap that moves such a row out of the group. In the lease form a crash with a row in work holds its group until that row's lease runs out. workers(n) gives no parallelism inside a group, so one worker serves a FIFO subscription, and a batch of a FIFO group holds one row. Groups run side by side, each through a subscription of its own. FIFO groups serve the row lock and the lease forms. In the advisory lock form a key on the group's field keeps one row of the group in work, and fifo = true beside advisory_lock does not compile. By hand, .fifo_group(..) names the group's column, and Fifo goes into the description's type.

A subscription by name, #[subscriber("emails")], reads the table its route leads to; it takes the broker's settings and no retry cap. A route, SqlxBroker::route::<Row>("emails"), leads a name into the table of a row type in both directions. A publish to the name writes a row through the row's Publish, and a subscription by the name reads that table. On a table with a group column the name selects its group, as an InboxQueue of the same name would. A name without a route stops the service at startup. A route leads only into a table in payload mode, so a subscription by name reads payload tables. It takes the broker's poll interval and lease, and refuses max_attempts(..) and dead_letter(..) at startup: an InboxQueue takes those. Where the route's row leaves every event to the crate and holds column types the crate reads itself, the subscription reads the rows by those columns, with no box and no dynamic call per message, in every form. Any other row runs its own code at one boxed delivery and one boxed settlement per message (NamedSubscriber). A subscription by name needs a dialect that implements ByName for its database, as every built-in dialect does.

on_threads runs an InboxQueue subscription's handlers on dedicated threads, each with a pool of its own, counted against connection_limit. It is the inbox's spelling of the framework's threads(n), for handlers that compute: it fills the position workers(n) fills, so the attribute names neither. InboxThreads::new(n) names the threads, by_key sends the rows of one partition key to one thread, and connections sets how many connections each thread opens, one unless set. The subscription claims on the app's runtime and runs each handler on one of its threads. Claims, settlements, transactions and publishes take the service's pool, and their connections open on the app's runtime. A handler's Ctx<keys::Pool<DB>> is the thread's own pool, with the service pool's options; its connections open on the thread and close when the thread ends. The service therefore opens its pool's connections and, for each such subscription, threads times connections. connection_limit(n) on the broker holds that sum to what the database allows: a subscription that would pass it stops the service at startup with SqlxBrokerError::ConnectionLimit. The framework's own threads(n) gives its threads pools of one connection too, and the limit does not count them. In the row lock form each delivery a thread holds keeps a connection of the service's pool, so the pool's bound applies as with workers(n) (Connections). A subscription by name takes the framework's threads(n).

A subscription claims while its claims come back full, then waits the poll interval, one second unless the broker or the queue sets another. InboxQueue::poll_interval sets the wait of one subscription, and SqlxBroker::poll_interval the wait of every subscription of the broker that sets none. A claim that found as many rows as it asked for is followed by the next one at once, so a backlog drains without a pause. A claim that found fewer waits the interval before the next one. A subscription by name takes the broker's interval. A publish through the broker into the subscription's table and group ends the wait at once, as Wake describes. So the interval bounds how long a row written by other means waits for its claim: a row another service inserts, a trigger writes, or the service writes with Insert. On Postgres listen_notify wakes a subscription for the rows of other processes too. A claim that fails is reported as an error of the subscription's stream, and the next claim waits one second. A shorter interval finds outside rows sooner, at the price of one more claim statement per interval and subscription.

workers(n) keeps a claim in flight for each free worker, bounded by the pool; with a partition_key column workers_by_key(n) keeps each key in order. A subscription with n workers runs up to n deliveries at once. It keeps a claim in flight for each free worker, so its workers take rows at once instead of one after another. It never holds more than the pool's size less one connection, so the pool keeps one for the handlers' own queries, their publishes and the settlements that take one (Connections). A subscription keeps one claim in flight where claims that run at once would cost more than they give. On SQLite, which takes one writer at a time, they only collide. On a table whose groups keep their order, or with a partition_key column, they could finish out of claim order. On MySQL and MariaDB a lease claim locks the rows it reads, leases in work included, until it commits. One claim in flight still feeds every worker: the next claim starts as soon as the last one returns. On SQLite a lease claim takes a row for every worker in one statement. The rows past the free workers wait in the subscription for the next free worker, and their leases are extended while they wait. Two claims never take the same row. How many workers a SQLite queue uses depends on what its handlers write. In the lease and advisory lock forms the throughput grows with the workers. In transactional mode a handler's first write takes the database's write lock, and the lock stays until the delivery settles. Every other writer then waits in SQLite's busy handler, which sleeps a millisecond or more instead of queueing it. A transactional subscription on SQLite whose handlers write gains little from a second worker in the lease form, and loses most of its throughput to these waits in the advisory lock form: it runs one worker there. A #[field(partition_key)] column holds each row's key: text or bytes, optional or not (KeyColumn). workers_by_key(n) sends the deliveries of one key to one worker, so the rows of a key are handled in the order they were claimed, and different keys run side by side. By hand, .partition_key(..) names the column, Key goes into the description's type, and the row reads its key through KeyRow.

#[derive(Inbox)] describes a queue table with an ordinary sqlx struct: the table in #[inbox(..)], column roles in #[field(..)], names from sqlx. The struct derives sqlx::FromRow beside Inbox, and the queue is a table of the service's own schema. #[inbox(table = "..")] names the table and is required; schema = ".." places it in a schema, and neither holds a dot. #[field(id)] marks the row's identity, the one role every table has; its type is Clone. The other roles, such as group, attempt and locked_until, each turn on one behaviour of the queue (Roles). sqlx's own attributes name the columns. A struct with a #[field(payload)] field is in payload mode, and one without it is in row mode. The rest of #[inbox(..)] selects how the table is served: Attribute What it does advisory_lock = "jobs-{id}" the advisory lock form, with a key built from the fields in braces isolation = .., mode = .. the isolation level or the SQLite mode the table's transactions open at clock = .. where "now" comes from custom(..) the events the service writes itself checked, db = .. the statements in sqlx's compile-time check A generic struct keeps its parameters: the impl asks Send + Sync + 'static of the struct and Clone + Debug + Send + Sync + 'static of the id field's type. A struct that cannot drive a queue does not compile, and the error points at the field or the name: no id, a role played twice, a column named twice, a dot in table, isolation beside mode, and the form rules of Events. The derive writes the InboxTable impl a table described by hand writes, and the traits its roles need.

One table holds the notifications of every channel: its channel column is the group, and each subscription reads the group its name selects. RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("notifier", "0.1.0")) // The table, created before the subscription checks it. .on_startup(async move |()| { let mut conn = SqliteConnection::connect(&schema_url).await?; sqlx::raw_sql(SCHEMA).execute(&mut conn).await?; conn.close().await }) .with_broker(broker, |b| { b.include(email); b.include(sms); }) } examples/manual/sqlx_tables_inbox.rs use chrono::{DateTime, Utc}; type Table = InboxSpec<(Attempt, Lease<DateTime<Utc>>, Payload)>; const TABLE: Self::Table = InboxSpec::new("notifications", Column::new("id").generated()) .group(Column::new("channel")) .attempt(Column::new("attempt").generated()) .lease(Column::new("locked_until")) .payload(Column::new("payload")); fn id(&self) -> &i64 { &self.id } } impl AttemptRow for Notification { type Attempt = i16; fn attempt(&self) -> &i16 { &self.attempt } } impl PayloadRow for Notification { type Column = Vec<u8>; fn payload(&self) -> &[u8] { &self.payload } } struct Deliver; #[inbox(checked, db = ..)] puts the statements a struct determines into sqlx's compile-time check against DATABASE_URL or the .sqlx offline data. db names the built-in dialect the statements are built with: postgres, mysql or sqlite. The derive builds them with the code the broker runs when a subscription opens, and wraps each in sqlx::query! inside a function nothing calls. The service's build then checks each statement against its database: a column the struct names and the table lacks fails the build. The subscription runs the statements it runs without checked, so a message costs the same. checked needs three things of the service: its own sqlx under the name sqlx, with the macros feature and the database's driver; DATABASE_URL at build time, or the .sqlx data that cargo sqlx prepare writes, committed beside the crate; SQLX_OFFLINE=true makes a build read that data even where DATABASE_URL is set, and cargo sqlx prepare --check fails a CI run whose data is stale; the feature of the dialect db names, on ruststream-sqlx. Each statement meets sqlx's own rules: with both chrono and time on, sqlx.toml names the preferred crate for time columns (sqlx's compile-time macros). The check covers every statement the struct determines: the claims, the guard of a FIFO group, the fetch after a claim of the service's own, the settlements, the dead letter of a group, the lease's extension and stamp, the advisory lock form's lock, unlock and take, and the generated insert. The startup check still runs, and still holds the move into a dead-letter table, which the mount names. In the headers layout checked goes on the headers struct, and the message reads its rows in a Fetch of its own, checked with sqlx::query!. A struct checked cannot cover does not compile, and the error points at the attribute or the field: checked without db or the reverse, a db whose feature is off, a #[sqlx(flatten)] field, a clock that is a parameter of the struct, the row lock form on SQLite, and checked on a message assembled from a headers struct. A dialect of the service's own keeps the startup check, because a procedural macro cannot run it.

The email queue of a Postgres service, its statements checked against the offline data in .sqlx. Its test runs on the Postgres stand that POSTGRES_TEST_URL names, and skips without it. examples/sqlx_tables_checked.rs /// Every statement this struct determines goes through sqlx's compile-time check. #[derive(Inbox, sqlx::FromRow)] #[inbox(table = "email_jobs", checked, db = postgres)] struct SendEmail { #[field(id, generated)] job_id: i64, #[field(group)] name: String, #[field(attempt, generated)] attempt: i16, #[field(payload)] payload: Vec<u8>, }

A column is named in one place, sqlx's attributes: rename, rename_all, raw identifiers and skip; a flattened field makes statements select every column. The derive reads a field's column name the way sqlx::FromRow reads it, so the statements and the struct never disagree. #[sqlx(rename = "..")] names a field's column as written. #[sqlx(rename_all = "..")] on the struct recases every other field's name. A raw identifier loses its r#: r#type reads the column type. A #[sqlx(skip)] field reads no column and plays no role. The other options of #[sqlx(..)], such as json, try_from and default, belong to sqlx's derive and pass through untouched. The dialect quotes every name in the statements it builds, so a name that needs quoting, a keyword or mixed case, reaches the database intact. A #[sqlx(flatten)] field reads columns the derive cannot see, so the statements select *. A dead-letter move into another table then copies the row by position, and the dead-letter table has the same columns in the same order. The headers layout is the exception: there a flattened field holds the headers struct, whose columns the derive sees. By hand, the description names each column as the table writes it, with Column::new, and .selecting_all() reads the table with *.

A queue in a table another system created: its id column is JobID, its group column is the keyword type, and its other columns are in camel case. Macros Manual examples/sqlx_tables_columns.rs #[derive(Inbox, sqlx::FromRow)] #[inbox(table = "LegacyJobs")] #[sqlx(rename_all = "camelCase")] struct LegacyJob { // `rename` names a column as written. #[field(id, generated)] #[sqlx(rename = "JobID")] job_id: i64, // A raw identifier loses its `r#`: the column is `type`. #[field(group)] r#type: String, // `rename_all` recases the rest: the column is `lockedUntil`. #[field(locked_until)] locked_until: Option<DateTime<Utc>>, #[field(payload)] body: Vec<u8>, } examples/manual/sqlx_tables_columns.rs #[derive(sqlx::FromRow)] struct LegacyJob { #[sqlx(rename = "JobID")] job_id: i64, body: Vec<u8>, } impl InboxTable for LegacyJob { type Id = i64; type Table = InboxSpec<(Lease<DateTime<Utc>>, Payload)>; const TABLE: Self::Table = InboxSpec::new("LegacyJobs", Column::new("JobID").generated()) .group(Column::new("type")) .lease(Column::new("lockedUntil")) .payload(Column::new("body")); fn id(&self) -> &i64 { &self.job_id } } impl PayloadRow for LegacyJob { type Column = Vec<u8>; fn payload(&self) -> &[u8] { &self.body } }

custom(..) hands one event of a table to the service's own SQL, Claim to Extend, and every other event keeps the statement the dialect builds. An event the table names, in #[inbox(custom(..))] on the derive or with .own::<own::X>() by hand, runs the service's own code in place of the dialect's statement. Each event is a trait the struct implements for its database: Event Trait What it does claim Claim selects and takes the ids of the next rows fetch Fetch reads the claimed rows, such as over a join ack Ack finishes a row its handler acknowledged retry Retry returns a row to the queue at once retry_after RetryAfter hides a row until a time discard Discard finishes a row its handler dropped dead_letter DeadLetter moves a row past its cap extend Extend extends the leases in work lock, unlock Lock, Unlock take and release the key of a row A named event without its impl does not compile, and the error names the trait. The table and the broker stay as they were, and every event the table does not name keeps the dialect's statement. A settlement of the service's own runs in the transaction the crate commits, so it settles the row as the built-in one does. An acknowledgement takes the row out of what the claim selects: a row it leaves claimable is delivered again. The form limits the events: the advisory lock form selects its candidates by key itself and takes no claim, extend belongs to the lease form, and lock and unlock come together in the advisory lock form.

A sent email stays in its table for an audit: the acknowledgement moves it to the sent group instead of deleting it. Macros Manual examples/sqlx_tables_events.rs use ruststream_sqlx::Ack; use sqlx::{Sqlite, SqliteConnection}; #[derive(Inbox, sqlx::FromRow)] #[inbox(table = "email_jobs", custom(ack))] struct SendEmail { #[field(id, generated)] job_id: i64, #[field(group)] name: String, #[field(locked_until)] locked_until: Option<DateTime<Utc>>, #[field(payload)] payload: Vec<u8>, } // A sent email stays in its table, in the `sent` group, for an audit. impl Ack<Sqlite> for SendEmail { async fn ack(conn: &mut SqliteConnection, id: &i64) -> Result<(), sqlx::Error> { sqlx::query("UPDATE email_jobs SET name = 'sent' WHERE job_id = ?") .bind(id) .execute(conn) .await?; Ok(()) } } examples/manual/sqlx_tables_events.rs use ruststream_sqlx::dialect::Column; use ruststream_sqlx::spec::{Lease, Payload, own}; use ruststream_sqlx::{Ack, InboxSpec, InboxTable, PayloadRow}; use sqlx::{Sqlite, SqliteConnection}; #[derive(sqlx::FromRow)] struct SendEmail { job_id: i64, payload: Vec<u8>, } impl InboxTable for SendEmail { type Id = i64; type Table = InboxSpec<(Lease<DateTime<Utc>>, Payload, own::Ack)>; const TABLE: Self::Table = InboxSpec::new("email_jobs", Column::new("job_id").generated()) .group(Column::new("name")) .lease(Column::new("locked_until")) .payload(Column::new("payload")) .own::<own::Ack>(); fn id(&self) -> &i64 { &self.job_id } } impl PayloadRow for SendEmail { type Column = Vec<u8>; fn payload(&self) -> &[u8] { &self.payload } } // A sent email stays in its table, in the `sent` group, for an audit. impl Ack<Sqlite> for SendEmail { async fn ack(conn: &mut SqliteConnection, id: &i64) -> Result<(), sqlx::Error> { sqlx::query("UPDATE email_jobs SET name = 'sent' WHERE job_id = ?") .bind(id) .execute(conn) .await?; Ok(()) } }

A table described by hand implements InboxTable: a const InboxSpec chain, its settings as types in type Table, and the same statements as the derive. The derive and the description by hand are two spellings of one public API, and they build the same statements and the same per-message code. A service writes the description by hand for a declaration a reviewer reads as it is, or for a struct that holds fewer fields than the table has columns. TABLE holds the description: InboxSpec::new takes the table's name and the id column, and each setter adds a setting. Every setter is a const fn, so the description is a constant and costs nothing at run time. type Id names the id's type, and fn id lends it off the row. type Table names the chain's final type, because stable Rust does not infer the type of an associated constant; a chain that does not match it is a type mismatch. The type lists the settings the crate reads, in the order the chain sets them: the form: Lease<Time> or Advisory; payload mode: Payload; the roles a delivery reads off a row: Key, Attempt, Headers, HeaderFields; the time roles with their time type: RetryAfter<Time>, ProcessedAt<Time>; Fifo, the clock Clock<Source> and the opening Opens<Level>; the events the service writes itself, the markers of spec::own. The column-only setters, within, group, priority, data, fetching and selecting_all, leave the type as it is. A setting the chain leaves out keeps its default: the row lock form, row mode, the host's clock, the database's own opening and the crate's events. Each role a delivery reads names a small trait the struct implements. Rule Derive By hand an id and a table name compile the constructor's arguments one form, one message mode, one clock, one opening; each typed role and each own event once compile the setter's bound, at compile time a role in the type has its trait; an own event is implemented compile a trait bound, at compile time the form rules of Events compile a bound on type Table, at compile time a column-only role set once; a column named once compile the constant's evaluation, at build time a lock key names a column the table has compile the statement's prepare, at startup A refusal at build time names the table and the rule, and points at the crate's check rather than the service's line.

One table, email_jobs, described twice: Welcome with the derive and Reminder by hand, each serving its own group. Insert writes a task with the derive's generated insert, inside the service's own transaction, so the task commits with the data it serves. The derive implements Insert for the connection of each enabled built-in driver: PgConnection, MySqlConnection and SqliteConnection. insert(&self, conn) writes every field of the struct but the generated ones: the roles, then the data columns, in the order the description lists them. A delayed task is a row whose retry_after lies ahead. The statement is built at compile time, and a call binds the fields and runs it on the connection it is given: a transaction of the service's own, or a handler's transaction. A headers struct gets the insert, and the message that flattens it gets none. A table described by hand writes its insert over the text dialect::insert renders from its description, in a constant of type Sql<N>. The text names every column the database does not fill, in the description's order, and the impl binds them in that order. A capacity N the text outgrows is a build error that names the size to raise it to. A row written this way wakes no subscription in the process: the subscription finds it on its next claim, at most a poll interval later. A publish through a route or a repository wakes the subscriptions of its table at once.

An order and the task that sends its receipt go into one transaction: both commit, or neither does. Macros Manual examples/sqlx_tables_insert.rs use sqlx::SqlitePool; #[derive(Inbox, sqlx::FromRow)] #[inbox(table = "receipt_jobs")] struct SendReceipt { #[field(id, generated)] id: i64, #[field(locked_until)] locked_until: Option<DateTime<Utc>>, #[field(payload)] payload: Vec<u8>, } /// Places an order and queues its receipt in one transaction: both commit, or neither does. async fn place_order(pool: &SqlitePool, order: &Order) -> Result<(), Box<dyn Error>> { let mut tx = pool.begin().await?; sqlx::query("INSERT INTO orders (id, total) VALUES (?, ?)") .bind(order.id) .bind(order.total) .execute(&mut *tx) .await?; let receipt = SendReceipt { id: 0, locked_until: None, payload: serde_json::to_vec(&Receipt { order: order.id })?, }; // `id` is generated: the insert leaves it to the database. receipt.insert(&mut *tx).await?; tx.commit().await?; Ok(()) } examples/manual/sqlx_tables_insert.rs use ruststream_sqlx::dialect::Column; use ruststream_sqlx::dialect::insert::{self, Sql}; use ruststream_sqlx::spec::{Lease, Payload}; use ruststream_sqlx::{InboxSpec, InboxTable, PayloadRow}; use sqlx::{SqliteConnection, SqlitePool}; #[derive(sqlx::FromRow)] struct SendReceipt { id: i64, payload: Vec<u8>, } impl InboxTable for SendReceipt { type Id = i64; type Table = InboxSpec<(Lease<DateTime<Utc>>, Payload)>; const TABLE: Self::Table = InboxSpec::new("receipt_jobs", Column::new("id").generated()) .lease(Column::new("locked_until")) .payload(Column::new("payload")); fn id(&self) -> &i64 { &self.id } } impl PayloadRow for SendReceipt { type Column = Vec<u8>; fn payload(&self) -> &[u8] { &self.payload } } // INSERT INTO `receipt_jobs` (`locked_until`, `payload`) VALUES (?, ?) const INSERT: Sql<128> = insert::sqlite(&SendReceipt::TABLE.spec()); impl Insert<SqliteConnection> for SendReceipt { async fn insert(&self, conn: &mut SqliteConnection) -> Result<(), sqlx::Error> { sqlx::query(INSERT.as_str()) .bind(None::<DateTime<Utc>>) .bind(&self.payload) .execute(conn) .await?; Ok(()) } } /// Places an order and queues its receipt in one transaction: both commit, or neither does. async fn place_order(pool: &SqlitePool, order: &Order) -> Result<(), Box<dyn Error>> { let mut tx = pool.begin().await?; sqlx::query("INSERT INTO orders (id, total) VALUES (?, ?)") .bind(order.id) .bind(order.total) .execute(&mut *tx) .await?; let receipt = SendReceipt { id: 0, payload: serde_json::to_vec(&Receipt { order: order.id })?, }; receipt.insert(&mut *tx).await?; tx.commit().await?; Ok(()) }

Each #[field(..)] role turns on one behaviour of the queue: group, priority, partition key, retry_after, attempt, processed_at, lease, headers, payload. A column that plays a role switches its behaviour on, and a table without it keeps the default: Role With the role Without it group a subscription reads the group its name selects; a dead letter moves the row to another group a subscription reads the whole table; a dead letter moves the row into another table group, fifo = true one row of a group is in work at a time, in claim order (FIFO) the rows of a group run side by side priority a smaller value is claimed first rows are claimed by retry_after where the table has it, then by id partition_key the delivery's partition key: under workers_by_key(n) the rows of one key run in order the delivery has no key retry_after retry_after(d) hides the row for d retry_after(d) returns the row at once, with a warning attempt Ctx<keys::Attempt> reads the count, and max_attempts(n) caps it Ctx<keys::Attempt> reads None, and a mount with max_attempts(n) stops at startup processed_at acknowledgement marks the row acknowledgement deletes the row locked_until the lease form the row lock form, or the advisory lock form under advisory_lock headers the delivery's headers, kept in one column the delivery's headers are empty payload payload mode: the handler takes the decoded payload row mode: the handler takes the row Every role but id is optional, and each plays on one column at most. generated beside a role marks a column the database fills in, such as a serial id or a column with a default, and the derive's insert leaves it out. By hand, each role is a setter of InboxSpec. A role a delivery reads off the row also names its marker in type Table and implements a small trait: Payload and PayloadRow, Key and KeyRow, Attempt and AttemptRow, Headers and HeaderRow. The roles only the queue reads, such as group, priority and processed_at, need no field in the struct.

The billing queue of a support table takes urgent tickets first, keeps each customer's tickets in order on one worker, and hides an open ticket for five minutes; an answered ticket stays in the table with its processed_at set. } HandlerOutcome::retry_after(Duration::from_secs(300)) } /// The service on the database `url` names. fn service(url: &str) -> RustStream { let schema_url = url.to_owned(); // Nothing connects here: the broker builds its pool when the service starts. let broker = SqlxBroker::from_url(url, SqlitePoolOptions::new()); RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("support", "0.1.0")) // The table, created before the subscription checks it. .on_startup(async move |()| { let mut conn = SqliteConnection::connect(&schema_url).await?; sqlx::raw_sql(SCHEMA).execute(&mut conn).await?; fn id(&self) -> &i64 { &self.id } } impl KeyRow for Ticket { type Key = String; fn partition_key(&self) -> &String { &self.customer } } impl AttemptRow for Ticket { type Attempt = i16; fn attempt(&self) -> &i16 { &self.attempt } } impl PayloadRow for Ticket { type Column = Vec<u8>; fn payload(&self) -> &[u8] { &self.payload } } struct Triage; impl Handle<Question> for Triage { fn handle( &self, question: &Question, _outs: &(), _ctx: &mut Context<'_>, ) -> impl Future<Output = Result<(), HandlerOutcome>> { if answer(question) { return ready(Ok(())); } ready(Err(HandlerOutcome::retry_after(Duration::from_secs(300)))) } } /// The service on the database `url` names. fn service(url: &str) -> RustStream { let schema_url = url.to_owned(); // Nothing connects here: the broker builds its pool when the service starts. let broker = SqlxBroker::from_url(url, SqlitePoolOptions::new()); RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("support", "0.1.0")) // The table, created before the subscription checks it. .on_startup(async move |()| { let mut conn = SqliteConnection::connect(&schema_url).await?; sqlx::raw_sql(SCHEMA).execute(&mut conn).await?; conn.close().await }) .with_broker(broker.route::<Ticket>("billing"), |b| { let triage = subscriber("billing", Triage) .map_source(|_| InboxQueue::<Ticket>::new("billing")) .workers_by_key(nonzero!(4)); TestApp::start runs the service against a real database, SQLite in memory for a start, with the harness waiting on every publish and a pausable clock. A test hands the harness the app main runs, unchanged, and addresses the broker by its production type, tb.broker::<SqlxBroker<Sqlite>>(). The testing feature in [dev-dependencies] adds the in-process mode and turns on the core's harness with it. The crate registers SqlxBroker<Postgres>, SqlxBroker<MySql>, SqlxBroker<Sqlite> and SqlxBroker<Any>; a broker on a dialect of the service's own is registered by the service. The in-process mode connects to the database the test's pool reaches, as connect does, because the service's SQL is part of what the test checks. SQLite needs no server: a database in memory named in a shared-cache URL serves every connection that names it, and lives while one of them is open, so the test holds one beside the pool. A test on Postgres, MySQL or MariaDB takes a database of its own on a server, with the service's migrations applied. The harness counts what reaches a queue and waits for it. A test's input goes in through the route and the service's Publish, as in production, and so do the service's own replies and slots. A publish through the harness returns once every handler it woke has settled, so the assertions that follow read finished state. A row is counted for the queue it lands in, its table and group, whatever name the subscription reads it by. A message published before its subscription opened waits in the table and is delivered once it opens. A row the service wrote with its own SQL before the test, a seed or a migration, is counted when its subscription opens, so settle waits for it as for a published message. A row written with the service's own SQL while the test runs is counted only once a claim takes it, so settle does not wait for it: such a test moves the clock past the poll interval with tb.advance. The queue reads "now" from a clock the test controls. After tokio::time::pause(), tb.advance(d) moves the queue's time by d, and a lease runs out or a delayed retry comes back when the clock passes it. The database calls run off that clock, so a paused clock does not jump while the database answers. A table on the database's clock reads the database's time, which the test clock does not move, and a clock of the service's own stays in force. Such a test, and one that needs what only a server has, runs live. A test build leaves the outbox off unless the switch turns it on.

TestApp::start_live runs the same test body on the real clock, against a database of the test's own on Postgres, MySQL or MariaDB. It connects the broker through its ordinary connect, and the queue reads the clock production reads. The body is the one an in-process test runs; only the start call differs. A publish, settle and advance wait on the real clock until every subscription has handled what was published to it, so tb.advance(d) lets d of real time pass. start_live refuses a paused clock. The live mode is for what the in-process mode leaves to the clock and to the server: a table on the database's clock, a clock of the service's own, the row lock form, isolation levels, listen_notify, and the MySQL and MariaDB specifics. Each test takes a database of its own on the stand and applies the service's migrations, so nothing an earlier run left is read. The repository's live tests read the stand's address from POSTGRES_TEST_URL, MYSQL_TEST_URL or MARIADB_TEST_URL, and return early without one, so cargo test passes on a machine with no stand. A job that stood the stand up sets RUSTSTREAM_REQUIRE_LIVE=1, and a missing address then fails the test instead of skipping it. The stand is docker-compose.test.yml, which just brokers-up starts. The examples of the Postgres and MySQL pages carry such tests.

The two tests share one body: one in process on a paused clock, one on the real clock, both over SQLite in memory. A queue reads "now" to claim, delay and mark rows; by default the host's SystemClock, bound in the column's own type as the service's inserts do. A claim compares "now" with retry_after and with the leases in work, a delayed retry writes "now" plus its delay, and an acknowledgement writes "now" into processed_at. A table that names no clock reads the host's system clock. The crate binds the time in the column's own type, so sqlx encodes it exactly as the service's own statements write times. The clocks of the hosts that serve one table are kept in step, well within a lease; keeping them in step is the hosts' concern, as NTP does. Where the hosts' clocks cannot be trusted, DatabaseClock makes the statements read the database's clock instead. A clock of the service's own takes the same place (Clock). Both are TimeSources: a host clock binds "now" into the statement, and the database's clock lets the statement read its own. In process a table on the system clock reads the tokio clock, anchored to the system clock when the broker connected. So a test on a paused clock moves the queue's time with tb.advance(d): rows come due and marks move with it.

An invoice the mail server cannot take returns in an hour by the host's clock, and a sent one is marked with the host's time. A clock of the service's own implements Clock and takes the place of SystemClock in clock = .. or .clock::<..>(), for every statement that reads "now". Clock has one function, now() -> SystemTime, and the crate turns its answer into each column's own type. #[inbox(clock = WholeSeconds)] names the clock on the derive; by hand .clock::<WholeSeconds>() names it, and Clock<WholeSeconds> goes into the description's type. The clock is a host clock, so every form takes it, the lease form included. Such a clock fits a service whose other tables keep times in a form of their own, whole seconds here, or a host that has to read a time other than its system clock's. A clock that is a type parameter of the struct is not taken by checked. In process the table reads its own clock, as in production, and a paused tokio clock does not move it.

clock = DatabaseClock makes the statements read the database's clock, so every host serving one table reads one clock; the lease form keeps the host's. With DatabaseClock the statements bind no time: each reads the database's own. Postgres reads statement_timestamp(), MySQL and MariaDB UTC_TIMESTAMP(6), and SQLite the current time as text. Every host that claims, delays or marks a row of the table then reads one clock, whatever its own says. The lease form reads the host's clock, because each settlement names the expiry its claim wrote, so locked_until beside clock = DatabaseClock does not compile. A table on the database's clock takes the row lock or the advisory lock form; on SQLite, which has no row locks, the advisory lock form. In process too the statements read the database's clock, which a paused tokio clock does not move, so a test of a delayed retry on such a table runs on the real clock with TestApp::start_live. By hand, .clock::<DatabaseClock>() names it, and Clock<DatabaseClock> goes into the description's type.

Statements written by hosts whose clocks drift wait a second by the database's clock when the month's figures are not closed yet. A time column holds chrono::DateTime<Utc> or time::OffsetDateTime; SQLite compares times as text, exact for chrono and to the second for time. QueueTime is the type a retry_after, processed_at or locked_until column holds: chrono::DateTime<Utc> under the chrono feature, time::OffsetDateTime under time. A field of such a role is the time or an Option of it (TimeColumn), and an optional one holds NULL until the crate writes it. The crate reads "now" and moves it forward in the column's own type, so sqlx encodes it exactly as the service writes times itself. SQLite keeps times as text, and a claim compares them as text. The text sqlx writes for a chrono time, RFC 3339 with +00:00, sorts as the times themselves. The text it writes for a time value ends in Z and drops the fraction's trailing zeros, so it sorts two times right only when they fall in different seconds. On SQLite a lease of a time table may therefore end up to a second late, and a delayed retry may come back up to a second early or late. By hand, the time type is a parameter of the description's markers, as in Lease<OffsetDateTime> and ProcessedAt<OffsetDateTime>.

}) }

.transactional() lends the handler its delivery's transaction: acknowledgement commits the handler's writes with the row's settlement, or neither. The handler takes the transaction as its first Ctx parameter, Ctx(mut tx): Ctx<keys::Tx<DB>>, and runs its statements through &mut *tx. A handler that takes keys::Tx on a subscription without the step does not compile, and the error names the step. Acknowledgement commits the handler's writes together with the row's settlement. Every other outcome rolls them back first, then settles the row as it would without the step; a retry still counts the attempt. A handler that panics while it holds tx commits none of its writes, even where its panic policy acknowledges the delivery. A delivery dropped unsettled closes its connection, and the server rolls its transaction back. A task the handler writes through tx into a queue table, with Insert or its own SQL, commits with the acknowledgement too. A write through keys::Pool commits on its own, whatever the outcome, and so does a publish through the broker. What the transaction is depends on the form: Form The handler's transaction row lock the claim's transaction, with a savepoint right after the claim that a settlement other than acknowledgement rolls back to lease a transaction of the delivery's own, opened once the claim committed; a lost lease rolls it back and the settlement fails with LeaseLost advisory lock a transaction on the session that holds the row's key, ended before the key's release Each of these transactions opens at the table's isolation level or SQLite mode. On SQLite a delivery's transaction takes the database's write lock at its first write and holds it until the delivery settles, keeping every other writer out, claims included. Each delivery in work holds a connection for its transaction, so a handler that takes a second one, through keys::Pool or a publish, needs a pool larger than its workers(n) (Connections). Transactional mode serves single deliveries: a batch handler mounted with .transactional() does not compile. The transaction goes back to the delivery when the handler's Tx drops; a settlement that finds it still out, in a task the handler moved it into, fails with TransactionHeld.

A signup opens its account and queues its welcome email through the delivery's transaction; when the CRM times out, the retry discards both, and the next attempt commits them. Macros Manual examples/sqlx_transactions.rs use ruststream_sqlx::prelude::*; use sqlx::Connection; use sqlx::sqlite::SqlitePoolOptions; use sqlx::{Sqlite, SqliteConnection}; /// One row of `signup_jobs`. #[derive(Inbox, sqlx::FromRow)] #[inbox(table = "signup_jobs")] struct OpenAccount { #[field(id, generated)] id: i64, #[field(attempt, generated)] attempt: i16, #[field(locked_until)] locked_until: Option<DateTime<Utc>>, #[field(payload)] payload: Vec<u8>, } /// One row of `welcome_jobs`, the mailer's queue. #[derive(Inbox, sqlx::FromRow)] #[inbox(table = "welcome_jobs")] struct SendWelcome { #[field(id, generated)] id: i64, #[field(locked_until)] locked_until: Option<DateTime<Utc>>, #[field(payload)] payload: Vec<u8>, } /// The account and its welcome email, written on the connection of the delivery's transaction. async fn open( conn: &mut SqliteConnection, signup: &Signup, ) -> Result<(), Box<dyn Error + Send + Sync>> { sqlx::query("INSERT INTO accounts (email) VALUES (?)") .bind(&signup.email) .execute(&mut *conn) .await?; let welcome = SendWelcome { id: 0, locked_until: None, payload: serde_json::to_vec(&Welcome { to: &signup.email })?, }; welcome.insert(conn).await?; Ok(()) } #[subscriber(InboxQueue::<OpenAccount>::new("signups"))] async fn open_account( signup: &Signup, Ctx(mut tx): Ctx<keys::Tx<Sqlite>>, Ctx(attempt): Ctx<keys::Attempt>, ) -> HandlerOutcome { if open(&mut tx, signup).await.is_err() { return HandlerOutcome::retry(); } if !register(signup, attempt).await { // The retry rolls the account and its welcome email back first. return HandlerOutcome::retry(); } // The commit keeps the account and its welcome email, and finishes the signup. HandlerOutcome::ack() } /// The service on the database `url` names. fn service(url: &str) -> RustStream { let schema_url = url.to_owned(); // Nothing connects here: the broker builds its pool when the service starts. let broker = SqlxBroker::from_url(url, SqlitePoolOptions::new()); sqlx::raw_sql(SCHEMA).execute(&mut conn).await?; conn.close().await }) .with_broker(broker.route::<OpenAccount>("signups"), |b| { b.include(open_account.transactional()); }) } examples/manual/sqlx_transactions.rs use ruststream_sqlx::prelude::*;
